name: Sol
etymology_summary: From the Puerta del Sol, one of Madrid's medieval fortress gates, first documented during the 1520 Comuneros revolt. The gate may have borne a carved sun or faced east toward the sunrise; it was demolished in 1570 but the name endured. The square became the symbolic heart of Spain: Kilometre Zero of the six national radial roads is marked in the pavement before the Casa de Correos. Since 1909, millions have gathered here on New Year's Eve to eat twelve grapes at midnight with each chime of the clock. The iconic Tio Pepe neon sherry sign has towered over the square since 1958, and the 1967 bronze statue of El Oso y el Madrono (the Bear and the Strawberry Tree), Madrid's heraldic emblem, is the city's most photographed monument.
source: Renfe Blog (renfe.com); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puerta_del_Sol; Secretos de Madrid

name: Gran Via
etymology_summary: Named after the Gran Via boulevard ('Great Way'), Madrid's iconic avenue built 1910-1929. Around 300 buildings were razed and fifteen streets erased to drive a 1.3 km east-west thoroughfare through the medieval core, a project contemporaries called 'an axe blow on the map'. First proposed by Carlos Velasco in 1886, it was the most ambitious urban transformation Madrid had seen since the 1860 Ensanche. After the Civil War the Franco regime renamed it Avenida de Jose Antonio after the Falange founder; Mayor Tierno Galvan restored the original name in 1981. Lined with early-20th-century theatres and cinemas, the Gran Via is often called Madrid's Broadway.

name: Tirso de Molina
etymology_summary: Named after Fray Gabriel Tellez (c. 1579-1648), known by his pen name Tirso de Molina, a Mercedarian friar and one of the great dramatists of the Spanish Golden Age. His play 'El burlador de Sevilla y convidado de piedra' (c. 1630) introduced the figure of Don Juan to world literature, a character reimagined by Moliere, Mozart, Byron, and countless others. Tellez entered the Order of Mercy at Madrid's Convento de la Merced Calzada around 1600, near where the plaza now stands. The metro station opened in 1921 as 'Progreso'; it was renamed Tirso de Molina in 1939 along with the plaza above, replacing the liberal-era name after the Civil War.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirso_de_Molina; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: La Latina
etymology_summary: Named after Beatriz Galindo 'La Latina' (1465-1534), a humanist so gifted in Latin that she lectured at the University of Salamanca before age twelve. Queen Isabel la Catolica summoned her to court as royal tutor; she went on to teach five queens, including Catherine of Aragon. She wrote Latin poetry and a commentary on Aristotle, and founded the Hospital de la Santa Cruz in Madrid in 1506. The neighbourhood where she lived still bears her nickname.

name: Goya
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco de Goya (1746-1828), court painter to the Spanish Crown and one of the most influential artists in Western history. A mysterious illness left him completely deaf in 1792, and in old age he painted his haunting Black Paintings directly onto the walls of his house near Madrid, never intending them for public display. Those murals were later transferred to canvas and moved to the Prado, where they remain among the museum's most visited works.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Goya; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Arguelles
etymology_summary: Named after Agustin de Arguelles (1776-1844), the liberal orator known as 'El Divino' for his eloquence in the Cortes of Cadiz. He drafted the Preliminary Discourse of the 1812 Constitution, championed press freedom, and fought to abolish torture and the slave trade. Ferdinand VII imprisoned him and drove him into eleven years of London exile, where he worked as a librarian rather than accept charity. He returned to serve as tutor to the young Queen Isabel II.

name: Chueca
etymology_summary: Named after Federico Chueca (1846-1908), the beloved zarzuela composer whose career began in prison: he composed a set of waltzes during three days jailed for joining a revolt, and the work so impressed Barbieri that it was orchestrated and staged. His 1886 masterpiece 'La Gran Via', a satirical revue of Madrid street life, ran four consecutive years and became a rare Spanish hit in Vienna and Paris. Today the vibrant neighbourhood around Plaza de Chueca also bears his name.

name: Embajadores
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Embajadores. During the reign of Juan II of Castile (15th century), a plague outbreak forced foreign ambassadors from Tunis, Navarre, Aragon, and France to be quartered in country houses outside the city walls to avoid contagion. The area became the 'Campo de Embajadores' (Field of Ambassadors), and the street leading to it inherited the name. Appears on the Texeira map (1656).
source: Secretos de Madrid; Wikipedia; Texeira map 1656

name: Lavapies
etymology_summary: Disputed origin. (1) Topographical theory (favoured by Lorenzo Arribas, CVC 2008; Bazaco Palacios et al. 2013): rainwater rushing down the steep barranco (ravine) toward Glorieta de Embajadores literally washed pedestrians' feet in the unpaved streets. The 2013 paper 'Lavapies, barranco y arrabal' characterizes the area as a dramatic ravine, not merely a slope. (2) Jewish fountain legend: Jews washed feet before entering a nearby synagogue. Modern historians reject this: Urgorri's 1954 study of the 1453 census shows Jews lived dispersed across Madrid, not in a ghetto. (3) Posada/inn theory: travellers washed feet before sharing beds. (4) Moratin's underground springs theory (dismissed by Mesonero Romanos). Earliest document: 1441 land sale mentioning 'two agricultural plots at Lavapies' (Archivo de Villa). Medieval variants: 'Alavapies'/'Avapies' (1441-1498).
source: Lorenzo Arribas (CVC 2008: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/noviembre_08/21112008_01.htm); Bazaco Palacios, Lorenzo Arribas & Real Gallego 2013 (academia.edu/4588123); Turra Historica 2021 (turrahistorica.com); Mesonero Romanos 'El antiguo Madrid' 1861; Madrid Archivo de Villa (earliest doc. 1441)

name: Chamberi
etymology_summary: Named after the neighbourhood, whose name derives from the French city of Chambery, capital of Savoy, though the transmission mechanism is debated. The most probable link is via Queen Barbara de Braganza, who founded the Royal Salesas Convent (c.1748) with nuns from Chambery/Annecy in Savoy; the toponym first appears on Chalmandrier's 1761 map. An alternative attributes it to Luisa Gabriela de Saboya (wife of Felipe V). The Napoleonic regiment theory is refuted by the 1761 map predating Napoleon. This station closed in 1966 and reopened as a museum ('Estacion Fantasma') in 2008.
source: Caridad Arias (dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=3012173); chamberi30dias.es/reportajes/chamberi-la-historia-del-nombre-frances-de-un-barrio-de-chisperos; Pedro de Repide; Chalmandrier map 1761 (IGN interactive viewer: ign.es/web/catalogo-cartoteca/resources/webmaps/chalmandrier.html; catalogue: ign.es/web/catalogo-cartoteca/resources/html/031304.html); Chamberi30dias; Ayuntamiento de Madrid 'Historia de Chamberi'

name: Callao
etymology_summary: Named after the plaza, which commemorates the 1866 naval Battle of Callao. On 2 May 1866, a Spanish squadron under Admiral Casto Mendez Nunez bombarded the Peruvian port of Callao in the final major engagement of the Chincha Islands War. When told the ironclad Numancia was endangered, Mendez Nunez reportedly declared 'Espana prefiere honra sin barcos que barcos sin honra' (Spain prefers honour without ships to ships without honour). The plaza, one of Madrid's busiest commercial intersections, was named in 1866 shortly after the battle.

name: Opera
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby Teatro Real (Royal Opera House), inaugurated on 19 November 1850 by Queen Isabel II with a performance of Donizetti's 'La Favorita'. Designed by Antonio Lopez Aguado and completed by Custodio Moreno, it was built on the site of the former royal washhouses. The theatre closed in 1925 due to structural problems and did not reopen until 1997 after a massive restoration. The station has had three different names: 'Isabel II' (1925-1931), 'Fermin Galan' (during the Republic/Civil War), and 'Opera' (from 1939).

name: Principe de Vergara
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Baldomero Espartero (1793-1879), who earned the title Principe de Vergara after brokering the Convention of Vergara on 31 August 1839, ending the First Carlist War with the famous 'Abrazo de Vergara' -- a public embrace with Carlist general Maroto before troops of both sides. During Franco's regime the street was renamed General Mola (1939); Mayor Tierno Galvan restored the original name in 1981, and the station followed in 1983.

name: Alfonso XIII
etymology_summary: Named after King Alfonso XIII (1886-1941), who did not merely inaugurate the first Metro line on 17 October 1919 but personally invested 1.45 million pesetas of his own money when no private bank except Banco de Vizcaya would back the project. He rode the first official train from Cuatro Caminos to Rios Rosas, a journey of just 40 seconds. The original line ran 3.48 km with eight stations.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfonso_XIII; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Gregorio Maranon
etymology_summary: Named after Gregorio Maranon y Posadillo (1887-1960), the physician-humanist who pioneered endocrinology in Spain and authored over 500 scientific monographs. His 'Manual of Etiologic Diagnostic' became one of the most widely distributed medical texts in the world. Equally prolific as a historian, he psychoanalyzed historical figures through a medical lens, writing landmark studies on Tiberius and the Count-Duke of Olivares from his Toledo cigarral.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gregorio_Mara%C3%B1%C3%B3n; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Paco de Lucia
etymology_summary: Named after Paco de Lucia (1947-2014), born Francisco Sanchez Gomez in Algeciras. His father, in a regimen compared to Leopold Mozart's, made him practise guitar up to twelve hours daily from age five. He took his stage name from his Portuguese mother Lucia, and his hit 'Entre dos aguas' — named for Algeciras, where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic — brought flamenco to a global audience. His collaborations with John McLaughlin and Al Di Meola fused flamenco with jazz.

name: Manuela Malasana
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby IES Manuela Malasana school, which is in turn named after Manuela Malasana Onoro (1791-1808), a young seamstress killed by French soldiers during the Dos de Mayo Uprising in Madrid. She was found carrying scissors which the French deemed a weapon, leading to her summary execution. She became a symbol of popular resistance against Napoleon.

name: Principe Pio
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Pio de Saboya (1659-1726), an Italian aristocrat and military commander who supported Felipe V during the War of Spanish Succession; his palace and gardens stood on the hill nearby. The Montana del Principe Pio became infamous on 3 May 1808, when French troops executed scores of Madrilenos in reprisal for the Dos de Mayo uprising against Napoleon's occupation. Francisco de Goya immortalised the scene in 'El tres de mayo de 1808', one of history's most powerful anti-war paintings, now in the Prado. The station was called Norte until 1994, when it was renamed to honour this layered site of aristocratic grandeur and popular resistance.

name: Eugenia de Montijo
etymology_summary: Named after Eugenia de Montijo (1826-1920), the Granada-born Spanish aristocrat who became Empress of France. When Napoleon III asked the path to her heart, she famously replied: 'Through the chapel, Sire.' Her family owned a palatial estate in Carabanchel where her mother hosted literary salons attended by Stendhal and Prosper Merimee. She died in Madrid in 1920 at the Liria Palace; in Carabanchel, only the ancient cypresses and the Estanque de las Brujas survive from her family's finca.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugenia_de_Montijo; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Guzman el Bueno
etymology_summary: Named after Alfonso Perez de Guzman 'el Bueno' (1256-1309), who defended Tarifa against a Moorish siege in 1294. When the rebel Infante Juan threatened to kill Guzman's ten-year-old son unless the fortress surrendered, Guzman threw down his own dagger from the ramparts, declaring he had not begotten a son to serve against his country. The boy was killed, yet Guzman held firm and the attackers withdrew. King Sancho IV named him 'el Bueno' -- the Righteous.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guzm%C3%A1n_el_Bueno; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Alonso Martinez
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Alonso Martinez (1827-1891), the Burgos-born jurist who believed a lawyer must also be a writer, studying both law and philosophy. He served as Minister of Justice, Finance, and Public Works, but his enduring legacy is the Spanish Civil Code of 1889, which he personally drafted according to twenty-six legal bases he devised. He also served as president of the Congress of Deputies.

name: Diego de Leon
etymology_summary: Named after Diego de Leon (1807-1841), 1st Count of Belascoain, the dashing cavalry officer known as 'la primera lanza del reino'. A hero of the First Carlist War, he led a failed 1841 pronunciamiento to restore the regent Maria Cristina. Condemned to death, he rode to the firing squad at the Puerta de Toledo in full dress uniform, distributed his cigarettes among those present, and reportedly commanded the squad himself, declaring: 'I do not die as a traitor.'
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_de_Le%C3%B3n; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Vicente Aleixandre
etymology_summary: Named after Vicente Aleixandre (1898-1984), poet of the Generation of '27 who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1977 for 'a creative poetic writing which illuminates man's condition in the cosmos.' Bedridden by illness for much of his life, he wrote from his home on Calle Velintonia 3, which became a literary salon where younger poets gathered. His house has been declared a Site of Cultural Interest. The station was renamed from 'Metropolitano' in 2018 as part of a broader effort to honour artists in the metro network.

name: Concha Espina
etymology_summary: Named after Concha Espina (1869-1955), the Santander-born novelist who was among the first Spanish women to support herself entirely through writing. She was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature 25 times across 28 years but never won. Blind for the last fifteen years of her life, she continued writing with the help of a ruled guideline. Her novel 'La esfinge maragata' won the Royal Academy's Fastenrath Prize in 1914.
source: Muy Interesante; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concha_Espina; RAH Diccionario Biografico Espanol

name: Santiago Bernabeu
etymology_summary: Named after Santiago Bernabeu (1895-1978), who presided over Real Madrid for 35 years (1943-1978), transforming it from a modest club into the most successful in European football history. Under his leadership, Real Madrid won the first five European Cups (1956-1960) with a legendary team featuring Di Stefano, Puskas, and Gento. The stadium bearing his name, opened in 1947 and expanded to 80,000+ seats, was named in his honour in 1955. The metro station was renamed from 'Lima' in 1997.

name: Estacion del Arte
etymology_summary: Renamed from Atocha on 1 December 2018 to eliminate passenger confusion with the nearby railway station and to celebrate Madrid's 'Triangulo del Arte': the Museo del Prado, Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza, and Museo Reina Sofia, all within walking distance. Together these three museums hold over 40,000 works spanning eight centuries. The station, which opened in 1921 on Line 1, is one of the oldest in the network and now features art-themed decorative panels.
named_after: Barrio de las Artes (Prado-Reina Sofia-Thyssen museum triangle)

name: Feria de Madrid
etymology_summary: Renamed from 'Campo de las Naciones' in 2017 to reflect its proximity to the IFEMA trade fair complex (Institucion Ferial de Madrid). IFEMA, founded in 1980, is one of Europe's largest exhibition venues, hosting events like FITUR (international tourism), ARCO (contemporary art), and the Madrid Fashion Week. The original name 'Campo de las Naciones' (Field of Nations) referenced the international character of the area, which also houses the Juan Antonio Samaranch Olympic Park. The station opened in 2002 on Line 8 connecting to Barajas Airport.

name: Estadio Metropolitano
etymology_summary: Renamed from 'Estadio Olimpico' in 2017 when Atletico de Madrid moved to the Wanda Metropolitano stadium (now Civitas Metropolitano) nearby. The stadium, designed by Cruz y Ortiz Arquitectos, was originally built for Madrid's failed 2012/2016 Olympic bids and adapted for football with a 68,456 capacity. It hosted the 2019 UEFA Champions League Final. The 'Metropolitano' name honours the historic Estadio Metropolitano (1923-1966), Atletico's original ground near Cuatro Caminos, itself named after the Metro company that funded it.

name: Atocha
etymology_summary: From the pre-Roman word *taucia meaning 'mata/matorral' (thicket/shrubland). 'Atocha' is a synonym for esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima) per the RAE. Corominas traces it through Mozarabic *attawca* back to pre-Roman *taucia, which also produced Galician-Portuguese 'touza'. First documented in the Fuero de Madrid (1202) as 'Prato de Toia' and in 1219 as 'Tocha'. The site became Spain's first railway terminus when the Madrid-Aranjuez line opened on 9 February 1851. The current station building, a stunning iron-and-glass structure by Alberto de Palacio (1892), now houses a famous tropical garden inside the former train shed. The station was the target of the devastating 11 March 2004 terrorist attacks.
source: CVC Cervantes; Corominas; eldiario.es; Fuero de Madrid 1202

name: Piramides
etymology_summary: Named after two 14-metre obelisks ('piramides') built in 1831 by architect Francisco Javier de Marietegui at the entrance to the Puente de Toledo. Despite the name, the structures are actually obelisks, not pyramids -- a misnomer that has persisted for nearly two centuries. The obelisks were designed as ornamental gateposts marking the approach to Pedro de Ribera's Churrigueresque bridge. The glorieta was formally named 'Glorieta de Piramides' on 28 December 1944; before that it was known as 'Glorieta del Puente de Toledo'.
named_after: Obelisks at Puente de Toledo (1831, by Francisco Javier de Marietegui)
source: Mirador Madrid; Wikipedia; El Diario de Madrid

name: Tribunal
etymology_summary: Named after the Tribunal de Cuentas (Court of Auditors), Spain's supreme audit institution, whose building (1863) is located on the street above. The Court reviews all government spending and has constitutional status. The station was originally called 'Hospicio' after the nearby Royal Hospice, a grand baroque building (1726) designed by Pedro de Ribera that housed orphans and the poor. The building now houses the Museo de Historia de Madrid with its spectacular Churrigueresque portal. The station connects Lines 1 and 10.

name: Noviciado
etymology_summary: Named after the Jesuit novitiate founded on 15 April 1602, when the Marquesa de Camarasa donated land that had been the abandoned Genoese Embassy. The complex occupied the block between San Bernardo, Noviciado, Amaniel, and Reyes streets, and its church was one of the largest Baroque temples in Madrid. After Charles III expelled the Jesuits in 1767, the building passed to missionary priests, then briefly back to the Jesuits, before becoming the Universidad Central in 1843.

name: Bilbao
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Bilbao roundabout, christened by municipal decree on 11 January 1837 to honour the Basque city of Bilbao for its heroic resistance during the First Carlist War. The site had earlier been the Puerta de los Pozos de la Nieve, where ice hauled by mule from the Sierra de Guadarrama was stored in 17th-century snow pits to chill drinks for Madrilenos. The Cafe Comercial, one of Madrid's oldest cafes (est. 1887), still overlooks the glorieta today.

name: Quevedo
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco de Quevedo (1580-1645), the Golden Age master satirist whose command of Spanish remains unrivalled. A skilled swordsman, he duelled the fencing master Pacheco de Narvaez and knocked his hat off on the first strike, igniting a lifelong feud. His vendetta with poet Gongora was even fiercer: Quevedo bought Gongora's rented Madrid house for the sole purpose of evicting him. He died in Villanueva de los Infantes after four years of political imprisonment.

name: Islas Filipinas
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Filipinas, honouring the Philippine Islands, Spain's colony from 1565 to 1898. The archipelago was named by explorer Ruy Lopez de Villalobos in 1543 after the future Philip II. Near the station, a 1996 replica of Manila's Rizal Monument stands in Parque de Santander -- donated by the Philippine government to honour Jose Rizal, the national hero whose 1896 execution helped ignite the Philippine Revolution.

name: Moncloa
etymology_summary: Named after the Moncloa district, whose name derives from 'Mons Clovis' (Mount of Clovis), likely transplanted from the Castillo de la Monclova estate in Seville by 17th-century courtiers. The Palacio de la Moncloa, rebuilt 1949-1953 after Civil War destruction, has served as the Prime Minister's residence since 1977. Nearby stands the 49-metre Arco de la Victoria, a controversial Franco-era triumphal arch inaugurated in 1956.

name: Ventas
etymology_summary: Named after Las Ventas, the area where the famous Plaza de Toros de Las Ventas bullring stands. 'Ventas' refers to the roadside inns (ventas) that once dotted this area on the road to Aragon. The bullring, designed by Jose Espelius in neo-Mudejar style, opened in 1931 with a capacity of 23,798 -- making it the largest bullring in Spain and one of the largest in the world. Every year, the San Isidro Festival (May-June) draws top matadors for a month-long series of corridas that defines the bullfighting season.

name: Manuel Becerra
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Becerra Bermudez (1820-1896), mathematician, engineer, and politician who served as minister under Amadeo I and Alfonso XII. Becerra was a prominent freemason who served as Grand Master of the Grand Orient of Spain, and his political career spanned the turbulent years of the Sexenio Democratico and the Restoration. The glorieta named after him is one of the busiest traffic intersections in eastern Madrid, where the Salamanca grid meets the older Guindalera neighbourhood.

name: O'Donnell
etymology_summary: Named after Calle O'Donnell, honouring Leopoldo O'Donnell (1809-1867), 1st Duke of Tetuan, general and prime minister of Spain. O'Donnell led the Liberal Union party and commanded the successful campaign in Morocco (1859-1860) that gave him his ducal title. The street was named when Madrid's medieval walls were demolished in 1868, opening the city to eastward expansion. The O'Donnell neighbourhood sits between the Retiro park and the Ibiza area, on land that was once just outside the old city walls.

name: Ibiza
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Ibiza, part of a cluster of Balearic Island street names -- including Menorca, Mallorca, Formentera, and Cabrera -- in Madrid's Retiro district. These names were established under the 1860 Castro Ensanche plan, which organised the city's eastward expansion into a grid. The neighbourhood itself is called Ibiza, making it one of the few Madrid barrios named after an island. Its tree-lined streets developed from the 1870s as an extension of the elite Salamanca district.

name: Pacifico
etymology_summary: Named after the former Calle del Pacifico (now Avenida de la Ciudad de Barcelona), which commemorated Spain's naval campaigns on South America's Pacific coast in 1865-1866. During the Chincha Islands War, a Spanish squadron bombarded Valparaiso on 31 March 1866, sinking 33 vessels, then attacked the fortified port of Callao on 2 May before withdrawing. The street name turned this controversial imperial episode into a lasting Madrid place name.
named_after: Spanish naval campaigns in the Pacific (1865)

name: Menendez Pelayo
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Menendez Pelayo, honouring Marcelino Menendez y Pelayo (1856-1912), a prodigious writer, philologist, and literary critic from Santander. By age 22 he held a university chair, and his 'History of Heterodox Spaniards' (1880-1882) made him the foremost authority on Spanish intellectual history. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature. The avenue runs along the western edge of the Retiro park, connecting Atocha with the Ibiza neighbourhood.

name: Rios Rosas
etymology_summary: Named after Antonio de los Rios Rosas (1812-1873), a jurist, orator, and liberal politician from Ronda (Malaga). Considered one of the most eloquent parliamentarians in 19th-century Spain, he served in multiple governments and was known for his principled defence of constitutional monarchy. His speeches were so admired that contemporaries compared him to Demosthenes. The station opened in 1919 as one of the original Line 1 stops, making it among the oldest in the network.

name: Iglesia
etymology_summary: Named after the Iglesia de Santa Teresa y Santa Isabel, a parish church built 1842-1856 near the Glorieta de Joaquin Sorolla (formerly Glorieta de Iglesia). The church served the rapidly growing Chamberi neighbourhood during Madrid's 19th-century expansion. The station was originally planned as 'Martinez Campos' (after the nearby street) but opened as 'Iglesia' in 1919. During the Civil War it was briefly renamed 'Sorolla' after the Valencian painter. It is one of the original Line 1 stations.
named_after: Iglesia de Santa Teresa y Santa Isabel
previous_names: Martinez Campos (planned but never used); Sorolla (Civil War era)

name: Cruz del Rayo
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Cruz del Rayo (1928-1929), the first Madrid colonia following Ebenezer Howard's garden city model. Legend: a stone cross ('cruz') on a stone pedestal was struck and deformed by lightning ('rayo'), giving the area its name. The colonia was promoted by the Real Institucion Cooperativa de Funcionarios del Estado and designed by Eduardo Ferres y Puig. BIC protection started 1978.
named_after: Cruz del Rayo (stone cross struck by lightning)

name: Prosperidad
etymology_summary: Named after the Prosperidad neighbourhood, itself named for Prospero Soynard y Polen, a 19th-century French-born landowner who acquired five acres of agricultural land south of the road to Hortaleza and subdivided them into small plots for sale. The neighbourhood was officially born on 14 December 1862 when the first two housing plots were notarised in the names of a bricklayer and a carpenter. Modest labourers, ragpickers, and immigrants from the interior flocked to buy cheap land on the urban fringe, giving La Prosperidad a distinctly working-class character. In 1898 it was absorbed into the Buenavista district and has belonged to Chamartin since 1955.

name: Cuatro Caminos
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta de Cuatro Caminos, a crossroads where four major roads converge: Bravo Murillo (north to Tetuan), Reina Victoria (northwest to Moncloa), Santa Engracia (south to Chamberi), and Raimundo Fernandez Villaverde (east to Nuevos Ministerios). Opened on 17 October 1919, it was the northern terminus of Spain's first metro line and the site of the original Metro depot and workshops. The iconic circular brick ventilation tower, still standing, is a protected industrial heritage monument.

name: Tetuan
etymology_summary: Named after the barrio of Tetuan de las Victorias, which commemorates Spain's victory in the Battle of Tetuan (6 February 1860) during the Spanish-Moroccan War led by General O'Donnell. The soldiers who fought in the campaign camped in this area north of Madrid upon their return, and the settlement that grew around their encampment took the name. 'Tetuan' itself derives from Berber 'Tittawin' (springs/eyes). The neighbourhood retains its military-themed street names: Bravo Murillo, General Margallo.

name: Estrecho
etymology_summary: Named after the local area which honours the Strait of Gibraltar (Estrecho de Gibraltar), continuing the neighbourhood's North African military nomenclature theme established when the Tetuan de las Victorias barrio was founded after the 1860 Morocco campaign. Nearby streets bear names like Bravo Murillo, General Margallo, and Castillejos, all referencing the same conflict. 'Estrecho' (strait) comes from Latin 'strictus' (tight/narrow). At only 14 km wide, the Strait of Gibraltar separates Europe from Africa and connects the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.

name: Valdeacederas
etymology_summary: Named after the historical street (now Capitan Blanco Argibay). 'Valdeacederas' means 'valley of the sorrels' (Rumex acetosa), a plant that grew abundantly in this low-lying area north of Madrid. The compound Val(le)+de+acederas follows the classic Castilian toponymic pattern where 'val-' contracts 'valle' (valley). Sorrel, with its distinctive sour taste (from Latin 'acidus'), was used in traditional cooking and folk medicine. The station opened in 1961 as part of Line 1's northward extension to Plaza de Castilla.

name: Francos Rodriguez
etymology_summary: Named after Jose Francos Rodriguez (1862-1931), a physician turned journalist who directed the Heraldo de Madrid (1902-1909). He served as mayor of Madrid in 1910-1912 and later as minister of Public Instruction. As president of the Madrid Press Association from 1922, he inaugurated its headquarters in the Palacio de la Prensa on Plaza del Callao in 1928. He was elected to the Real Academia Espanola in 1924 and also wrote plays under the pen name Juan Palomo.

name: Carpetana
etymology_summary: Named after Via Carpetana, which references the Carpetani, a pre-Roman Celtic people who inhabited central Iberia including the area of modern Madrid from the 4th century BC. The Carpetanos lived in fortified hilltop settlements (oppida) along the Manzanares, Jarama, and Tajo rivers, including the Cerro de la Gavia site near Vallecas. During station construction works in 2008, remarkable paleontological remains over 14 million years old (Miocene period) were discovered, including fossils of mastodons and rhinoceroses. These are now exhibited in the station's 'Andenes de Dinosaurios' museum.

name: Oporto
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Oporto, which references the Portuguese city of Porto (Oporto in Spanish). The 'O' in 'Oporto' is actually the Portuguese definite article 'o' fused with 'Porto' (port/harbour). The street naming is part of Madrid's tradition of honouring significant European cities. The station, opened in 1968, sits at the intersection of Lines 5 and 6 in the Carabanchel district, one of the densest and most diverse neighbourhoods in southern Madrid.

name: Vista Alegre
etymology_summary: Named after the Vista Alegre neighbourhood, which takes its name from the Quinta de Vista Alegre ('Joyful View Estate'), a royal estate purchased by Queen Maria Cristina of Bourbon in 1832 as a country residence. The 'joyful view' refers to the panoramic vistas of the Manzanares valley from the estate's elevated position. The palace and its extensive gardens became a centre of court life. Today the grounds house the Vista Alegre bullring (built 1904), one of two bullrings in Madrid alongside Las Ventas.

name: Carabanchel
etymology_summary: Named after the Carabanchel district, formerly two independent municipalities (Alto and Bajo). The most accepted etymology traces it to the pre-Roman/Indo-European root *kar-/*karav- meaning 'stone' (per Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromana Hispana 1953), describing 'stony ground'. Menendez Pidal links it to Garabandal (Cantabria) as a variant, both from *carau-*. The earliest documented form is 'Caravangiel/Caravanchel' (1 January 1181, original parchment in Archivo de la Catedral de Toledo); 'Carauanchiel' appears in 1264. Alternative theories: Arabic 'carab' (cultivable land owner, per Oliver Asin); 'garbanzal' (chickpea field -- the area was famed for excellent chickpeas); the Illyrian anthroponym Caravantius with diminutive Carabancilius (per Caridad Arias 2004). The Mozarabic variant 'Caramanchel' appears through B/M alternation.
source: Menendez Pidal, Toponimia Prerromana Hispana 1953; Caridad Arias (Anales IEM 44, 2004, pp. 821-830: dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=3012173); Oliver Asin; Archivo Catedral de Toledo (1181 doc); karabanchel.com; celtiberia.net/es/poblamientos/?id=799

name: Arturo Soria
etymology_summary: Named after Arturo Soria y Mata (1844-1920), visionary urbanist who designed the Ciudad Lineal (Linear City) concept in Madrid, a pioneering model of urban planning built 1892-1911. In 1894 he founded the Compania Madrilena de Urbanizacion to realise his idea of a narrow, tramway-centred ribbon city stretching from Fuencarral to Vallecas. In 1897 he launched 'La Ciudad Lineal', considered the world's first journal devoted to urbanism, which he published until 1932 and which influenced Frank Lloyd Wright and Le Corbusier. Though only a 5 km fragment was built, the concept inspired linear-city projects across Europe and Latin America.

name: Esperanza
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Virgen de la Esperanza housing development, built 1965-1971 by the Cooperativa Virgen de la Esperanza. The development, designed by architects Antonio Camunas Paredes and Jose Antonio Camunas Solis, comprised 3,393 homes for working-class families. Streets were named after towns in Teruel province (Andorra, Calanda, Alcorisa, Utrillas), reflecting the Aragonese origins of many residents who migrated to Madrid during the 1960s rural exodus. The parish of Virgen de la Nueva serves the community.

name: Canillas
etymology_summary: Named after the village of Canillas, first documented in a 1252 land-purchase deed. For centuries it was an agricultural hamlet of cereal fields and vineyards producing local garnacho wine; Philip II's 1579 census counted just 50 households. Annexed to Madrid by decree on 17 August 1949, the village was soon transformed as the State built absorption settlements to house rural migrants flooding the capital during the postwar boom.

name: Mar de Cristal
etymology_summary: Named after the Glorieta Mar de Cristal roundabout in the Hortaleza district. The origin of the poetic name 'Sea of Crystal' is undocumented -- it may be a biblical reference (Revelation 4:6) or a decorative urbanistic name from the 1980s-90s Hortaleza development. No historical document or planning record explaining the naming has been found.

name: Chamartin
etymology_summary: Named after the former municipality of Chamartin de la Rosa, annexed to Madrid in 1948. The name likely derives from Basque: 'Echa-Martin' (estate of chief Martin), from Basque 'aita' (father/chief) with initial vowel lost through apheresis, documented as 'Echamartin' in 1247. The Toponomasticon Hispaniae confirms this as an established repopulation-era toponym. Chamartin was a rural village until the 20th century; its transformation began when the railway station was built in 1967 (now Madrid's second-largest, handling AVE high-speed trains). Napoleon established his headquarters here in December 1808.

name: Colombia
etymology_summary: Named after the South American country of Colombia. Located in the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood of the Chamartin district, where many streets are named after Latin American countries and locations -- a pattern reflecting Spain's deep historical ties to its former colonial territories. Nearby stations include Republica Argentina and Cuzco, creating a distinctively Latin American-themed section of northern Madrid. The station opened in 1982 and connects Lines 8 and 9.

name: Nuevos Ministerios
etymology_summary: Named after the Nuevos Ministerios government complex, designed by architect Secundino Zuazo Ugalde and sponsored by Minister of Public Works Indalecio Prieto during the Second Republic. Construction began in 1933 on the site of the former hippodrome (racetrack) but was interrupted by the Civil War. The buildings were not completed until 1942 under Franco's regime, which repurposed Zuazo's modernist design for its own bureaucratic needs. The station is one of Madrid's busiest transport hubs, connecting three metro lines with the Cercanias commuter network.

name: Ruben Dario
etymology_summary: Named after Ruben Dario (1867-1916), born Felix Ruben Garcia Sarmiento in Nicaragua, the poet who single-handedly founded Modernismo and revolutionized Spanish-language verse on both sides of the Atlantic. He first visited Madrid in 1892 as a Nicaraguan delegate and dazzled a circle of young writers including Juan Ramon Jimenez and Valle-Inclan. His 1905 masterwork 'Cantos de vida y esperanza', published in Madrid, is considered among the finest poetry collections in the Spanish language.

name: Nunez de Balboa
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Vasco Nunez de Balboa (1475-1519), the Spanish explorer who was the first European to sight the Pacific Ocean from the Americas. On 25 September 1513, after crossing the Isthmus of Panama, Balboa waded into the sea in full armour and claimed the ocean for Spain. Despite this achievement, he was later executed on false charges of treason by his rival Pedro Arias Davila. The Calle de Nunez de Balboa runs through the heart of the upscale Salamanca district.

name: Barajas
etymology_summary: Named after the district of Barajas, a former independent town annexed to Madrid. (1) Bar Axa theory: Philip II's 1575 Relaciones topograficas record that 'en tiempo que los moros, fue senor de este pueblo un moro llamado Baraja, hijo de una mora llamada Aja'. Covarrubias (Tesoro 1611) supports this, noting 'Axa' could be Hebrew (daughter of Caleb) or Arabic ('the adorned one'). (2) Latin *varalia* (fence of crossbars) per Nieto Ballester (1997). (3) Latin *uaralia* (quarrel/litigation) per Gutierre Tibon -- different semantic value from Nieto's proposal. (4) Pre-Roman toponym or ethnonym per Caridad Arias (Anales IEM XLVII, 2007), with parallels across the Peninsula and Gaul.
source: Philip II Relaciones topograficas 1575; Covarrubias, Tesoro de la lengua 1611; Nieto Ballester, Breve diccionario de toponimos espanoles 1997; Caridad Arias (Anales IEM XLVII, 2007); Isabel Gea; cvc.cervantes.es/foros/leer_asunto1.asp?vCodigo=45869

name: Canillejas
etymology_summary: Named after Canillejas, a village whose name derives from 'canillejas', the diminutive of 'canilla' (pipe or spigot), referring to the underground water conduits that distributed water through the area's fountains. First documented in the 13th century, the village received a royal tribute exemption from Alfonso X in 1274 for aiding Castile during the Reconquista, a privilege renewed by Alfonso XI in 1330. In the 16th century Canillejas lost its special status after joining the Comuneros revolt against Charles I, though it retained a papal indulgence for the feast of Santa Maria la Blanca. It remained an independent municipality, surrounded by aristocratic estates, until its annexation to Madrid on 24 June 1949.

name: Torre Arias
etymology_summary: Named after the Quinta de Torre Arias, a noble country estate whose origins date to around 1580, when the first Count of Villamor, Garcia Alvarado Velasco, built a country house in the village of Canillejas during the reign of Felipe II. In the 17th century the Count of Frigiliana doubled the estate's size, adding gardens, stables, and a stone staircase descending to formal grounds. During the War of the Spanish Succession the property was confiscated by the Archduke of Austria's troops for his residence. By the late 18th century it had passed to the VI Count of Torre Arias, giving the estate the name it bears today. Its last private owner, Tatiana Perez de Guzman el Bueno, donated it to Madrid City Council in 1986; it was declared an Asset of Cultural Interest in 2022.

name: Legazpi
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Legazpi, honouring Miguel Lopez de Legazpi (1502-1572), the Basque conquistador who led the expedition to colonise the Philippines and became the first governor-general of the Spanish East Indies. Legazpi established Manila as the colonial capital in 1571, creating the famous Manila Galleon trade route that connected Asia with the Americas for 250 years. The plaza sits at the confluence of the Arganzuela and Usera districts, near the former Matadero (slaughterhouse), now a major arts centre.

name: Delicias
etymology_summary: Named after the Paseo de las Delicias ('Promenade of Delights'), a tree-lined avenue leading to the Manzanares River. The name dates to the reign of Ferdinand VI (1746-1759), when two promenades were laid out along the river and called 'las Delicias del rio' for the pleasant gardens lining the embankment. Under Charles III the promenade was extended to form a Baroque trident radiating from what is now Plaza del Emperador Carlos V. The painter Bayeu captured its lively late 18th-century atmosphere in a painting now at the Prado. The nearby Delicias railway station, designed by French engineer Emile Cachelievre in an innovative iron-and-glass structure, was inaugurated on 30 March 1880 to serve the line to Ciudad Real and Portugal; it has housed Madrid's Railway Museum since 1984.

name: Mendez Alvaro
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Mendez Alvaro (1806-1883), a physician and hygienist who took the first measures against cholera and plague epidemics in Madrid and helped organize Spain's national vaccination centre. He was awarded the Cruz de Epidemias and rose to president of the Royal Academy of National Medicine. His political career was briefer: he served as mayor of Madrid in 1843 for barely one month.

name: Palos de la Frontera
etymology_summary: Named after the town of Palos de la Frontera in Huelva province, from where Columbus set sail in 1492. The station was originally called 'Palos de Moguer' due to a historical error that confused the towns of Palos de la Frontera and Moguer; corrected in 1986.

name: Pavones
etymology_summary: Named after the Pavones neighbourhood in the Moratalaz district, under the Calle de la Hacienda de Pavones. The name 'Pavones' likely derives from an old estate (hacienda) in the area. The neighbourhood was urbanized in the 1960s-1970s as part of the massive expansion of eastern Madrid. Moratalaz, once a rural dehesa (pastoral common) belonging to the Order of Calatrava, was transformed into one of Madrid's most densely populated residential districts. The station opened in 1980 on Line 9.

name: Valdebernardo
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdebernardo neighbourhood in Vicalvaro, meaning 'Valley of Bernardo' after Bernardo Gomez, a Barcelonian ancestor of the former landowner. Planned as a PAU (Programa de Actuacion Urbanistica) from the 1980s and assumed by the regional government in 1989, the area was formally constituted as an independent neighbourhood only in 2017 after an administrative reorganisation by the Ayuntamiento de Madrid.

name: Vicalvaro
etymology_summary: Named after the historic town of Vicalvaro, annexed to Madrid in 1951. From 'Vico Alvaro' = Alvaro's village (Latin 'vicus' + personal name). The earliest known document mentioning the settlement dates to 1352 in the Vatican Archives. Vicalvaro entered Spanish history books on 28 June 1854, when General Leopoldo O'Donnell launched the 'Vicalvarada' against the moderate government of Isabel II. The battle was inconclusive, but O'Donnell's young adviser Antonio Canovas del Castillo drafted the Manifesto of Manzanares, which rallied popular support and toppled the cabinet, ending the Moderate Decade and opening the Progressive Biennium (1854-1856).

name: San Cipriano
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de San Cipriano in Vicalvaro, honouring Saint Cyprian of Carthage, a 3rd-century bishop martyred by beheading in 258 AD. His name derives from Latin 'Cyprianus' (from Cyprus). The street is one of the oldest in Vicalvaro's historic core, already marking its boundary on the 1900 Facundo Canada map alongside the Valderribas cement factory. Vicalvaro's parish church, Santa Maria la Antigua, is first documented in 1427 and was expanded by order of Philip II in 1590, though no ermita dedicated specifically to San Cipriano survives. The earliest known mention of the settlement itself dates to 1352, in a Vatican archive document recording tithes.

name: Hospital 12 de Octubre
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario 12 de Octubre, one of Madrid's largest public hospitals. Originally inaugurated by Franco on 2 October 1973 as 'Ciudad Sanitaria 1 de Octubre', the name commemorated his appointment as Head of State on 1 October 1936. The X-shaped building, designed by Martin Jose Marcide on a 178,000 m2 plot in southern Madrid, was built in just eighteen months. After the dictator's death, the hospital was renamed '12 de Octubre' in 1988, shifting the reference to Spain's National Day (Dia de la Hispanidad), which commemorates Columbus's arrival in America in 1492. It became a university hospital linked to the Complutense shortly after opening and today is one of Europe's leading teaching hospitals.

name: Almendrales
etymology_summary: Named after the Almendrales neighbourhood. Around 1954 the owner of these lands planted with almendros (almond trees) sold the rural parcels to immigrants. The area was historically known as 'cerro de los Almendros'. The Colonia Los Almendrales was built 1942-1945.

name: Usera
etymology_summary: Named after the Usera district, which takes its name from Colonel Marcelo Usera, a middle-class military officer and agricultural entrepreneur. After marrying Carmen del Rio Fernandez, he inherited extensive land in Carabanchel and between 1925 and 1930 subdivided it into affordable housing plots for working-class families. His administrator laid out the new streets, naming many after members of the Usera family -- Isabelita, Amparo, Gabriel -- giving the neighbourhood an almost dynastic character. During the 1940s-50s Madrid's expansion absorbed the colony, and Usera was formally constituted as a district in 1987. Since the 2000s it has been transformed by the arrival of a large Chinese community, becoming Madrid's de facto Chinatown.

name: Plaza Eliptica
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza Eliptica roundabout, so called because of its distinctive elliptical shape. Located at the junction of the Usera and Carabanchel districts, it has been one of Madrid's busiest traffic nodes since its construction. The station opened in 1981 as the terminus of Line 6 and later became a key interchange when Line 11 was added in 2006. The plaza connects the radial avenues of Oporto and General Ricardos with the Paseo de Santa Maria de la Cabeza.

name: Puerta de Arganda
etymology_summary: Named as a gateway ('puerta') to the municipality of Arganda del Rey, marking the point where the metro exits Madrid's municipal territory. 'Arganda' derives from the Indo-European root *arg- meaning 'bright/white' (related to Latin argentum, silver), per Garcia Sanchez (CVC 2007). The 'del Rey' suffix was added in 1996 to honour Philip II's 1583 purchase of the town from the Archbishopric of Toledo. The Line 9 extension to Arganda was built partly along the old Tren de Arganda railway route.

name: Arganda del Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of Arganda del Rey. 'Arganda' derives from the Indo-European root *arg- meaning 'white/bright' (related to Latin argentum: silver), per Garcia Sanchez (CVC 2007), describing the clear waters of the area's streams. 'Del Rey' was added in 1996, honouring Philip II's 1583 purchase of the town from the Archbishopric of Toledo. Arganda's vineyards produce wines under the D.O. Vinos de Madrid. The Line 9 extension to Arganda was partly built along the old Tren de Arganda route, immortalised in the popular song 'que pita mas que anda'.

name: La Poveda
etymology_summary: Named after the La Poveda neighbourhood of Arganda del Rey. 'Poveda' derives from Latin 'populus' via 'alameda' (poplar grove), referencing the poplar trees that lined the Jarama and Tajuna river valleys. The neighbourhood grew around the Azucarera de Madrid sugar factory, founded in 1899 after Spain lost Cuban sugar production; its guard house (1900) still stands as a heritage interpretation centre. Wine has been cultivated in Arganda since Roman times on its clayey riverside soils, and the famous Tren de Arganda -- immortalised in the saying 'pita mas que anda' (whistles more than it moves) -- carried both wine and passengers to Madrid from 1886. Today Arganda belongs to the Vinos de Madrid DO (est. 1990), and its fertile vega historically supported cherry orchards alongside the vineyards.

name: Tres Olivos
etymology_summary: Named after the Tres Olivos residential area in Fuencarral-El Pardo. 'Tres Olivos' means 'Three Olive Trees', a toponym referencing olive trees that once marked this location. The area was developed in the 1990s as part of the urban expansion north of Madrid, preceding the nearby PAU developments. The central plaza is called 'Plaza de los Tres Olivos', from which four roads radiate connecting to the surrounding neighbourhoods of Montecarmelo, Las Tablas, and Fuencarral.

name: Montecarmelo
etymology_summary: Named after the PAU (urban development) of Montecarmelo, itself named for the Arroyo de Montecarmelo, a stream evoking Mount Carmel in Israel, sacred to the Carmelite order. The stream rises near the Ermita de Nuestra Senora de Valverde, where tradition holds that an image of the Virgin was miraculously found on 25 April 1242 by shepherds from Fuencarral who saw a light emanating from a retama bush. The sanctuary was declared a Bien de Interes Cultural in 2021. The PAU was developed under the 1997 General Plan.

name: Las Tablas
etymology_summary: Named after the PAU (Programa de Actuacion Urbanistica) of Las Tablas, one of the large-scale residential developments approved under Madrid's 1997 General Plan. 'Tablas' in its agricultural sense means flat, rectangular plots of cultivable land -- a fitting description of the open terrain that existed here before urbanisation began in the early 2000s. The neighbourhood is now home to the Distrito Telefonica campus (Distrito C), a 390,000 m2 corporate headquarters designed by Rafael de La-Hoz and inaugurated in 2008, housing some 14,000 employees and one of Europe's largest rooftop solar arrays.
source: RAE (dle.rae.es/tabla -- agricultural: strip of cultivable land); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Tablas_(Madrid); inmoversion.es; comunidad.madrid

name: Pinar de Chamartin
etymology_summary: Named after the pine grove ('pinar') of the former municipality of Chamartin de la Rosa. In December 1808, Napoleon camped nearby at the Ducal Palace of Infantado for twenty pivotal days, during which he issued decrees abolishing the Inquisition and feudal institutions. Legend holds he would walk to the pinar and meditate beneath a great pine tree -- the famous 'Pino de Napoleon', first photographed by Laurent in 1898 and lost to M-30 motorway construction around 1975. The Dukes of Pastrana had donated the estate to the Jesuits in 1879.
named_after: Pinar de Chamartin (pine grove of Chamartin)

name: Anton Martin
etymology_summary: Named after Anton Martin (c. 1500-1553), a farmer from Mira (Cuenca) who became the first companion and successor of San Juan de Dios. Remarkably, he joined the Order after forgiving his own brother's murderer at San Juan de Dios's urging. In 1552 he founded the Hospital de Nuestra Senora del Amor de Dios on Calle de Atocha, initially with twenty beds for the incurable. By 1587 it became Madrid's largest hospital. He died of pneumonia on Christmas Eve 1553.

name: Retiro
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque del Buen Retiro, one of Madrid's most beloved landmarks. The park originated in the 1630s as a royal pleasure ground for King Felipe IV, designed by the Count-Duke of Olivares as an escape from court protocol. The name 'retiro' (retreat) traces to the San Jeronimo el Real monastery where monarchs retired during Lent. The park's Crystal Palace (1887), modelled on London's, was built for a Philippine Exposition. The park was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021 as part of the 'Landscape of Light' designation. The station opened in 1924.

name: Banco de Espana
etymology_summary: Named after the Bank of Spain (Banco de Espana) building, the country's central bank, located adjacent to the station at the Plaza de Cibeles. The neoclassical building was designed by Eduardo Adaro and Severiano Sainz de la Lastra and inaugurated in 1891. It houses one of the world's most secure gold vaults, built deep into the bedrock beneath the Cibeles fountain. The station opened in 1924 as one of the original Line 2 stops and sits at the heart of Madrid's financial and institutional district.

name: Sevilla
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Sevilla, a short street running from Plaza de Canalejas to Calle de Alcala. It was formerly known as Calle Ancha de los Peligros ('Wide Street of Perils'). The street became a fashionable axis in the late 19th century: the Cafe Suizo opened at its end in 1846, and the Palacio de la Equitativa and Banco Hispano Americano (1902) defined the Alcala intersection. The metro station opened on 14 June 1924 as one of the original Line 2 stops.

name: Santo Domingo
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Santo Domingo, which references the Dominican convent of Santo Domingo el Real. Founded in 1218 by Fray Pedro de Madrid and Fray Suero Gomez as a male house, it was converted to a female convent two years later when Saint Dominic de Guzman himself visited Madrid. For over six centuries it was one of the city's most powerful religious institutions; Pedro the Cruel reportedly executed enemies within its walls. After the 1868 Gloriosa revolution, the new anticlerical municipal government demolished the convent in 1869 and expelled the nuns, who eventually resettled on Claudio Coello street in 1882, where their community endures today.
named_after: Convento de Santo Domingo el Real

name: San Bernardo
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de San Bernardo, which honours Saint Bernard of Clairvaux. A Cistercian monastery dedicated to him, founded in 1617 by Cardinal Bernardo Sandoval y Rojas, once stood nearby and boasts the largest oval dome in Spain. The street also housed the Jesuit Noviciado from 1602, which after the 1767 Jesuit expulsion was converted in 1843 into the Universidad Central -- making this one of Madrid's great academic axes.

name: Canal
etymology_summary: Named after the Canal de Isabel II water infrastructure, Madrid's main water supply system. In 1851, Queen Isabel II approved the ambitious project to bring water from the Lozoya River in the Sierra de Guadarrama, 70 km north of Madrid, through a canal and aqueduct system. The Third Reservoir (Tercer Deposito), built 1907-1915 near this station, is an architectural marvel -- a cavernous underground structure supported by over 1,500 columns that has been compared to a subterranean cathedral. Today the Canal de Isabel II manages water for 6 million people.

name: Ventura Rodriguez
etymology_summary: Named after Ventura Rodriguez Tizon (1717-1785), one of Spain's most important 18th-century architects. Largely self-taught, he rose to become Chief Architect of the Royal Works under Carlos III. He designed the Fuente de Cibeles and Fuente de Neptuno -- Madrid's two most iconic fountains -- as well as numerous churches and palaces across Spain. His rivalry with the Italian architects favoured by the Bourbon court (especially Sabatini) defined an era of Spanish architecture. The station opened in 1941.

name: Puerta de Toledo
etymology_summary: Named after the Puerta de Toledo, the last monumental gate built in Madrid (completed 1827). Designed by Antonio Lopez Aguado as a triumphal arch, it was originally conceived during the Napoleonic occupation to honour Joseph Bonaparte. After the French were expelled, the design was repurposed to celebrate King Fernando VII's return. This ironic reversal -- a gate initially planned for an enemy king -- makes it unique among Madrid's monuments. The neo-classical arch features allegories of Spain and its provinces.

name: Acacias
etymology_summary: Named after the Paseo de las Acacias (Acacia Walk), a tree-lined promenade in the Arganzuela district south of the city centre. The paseo was planted with rows of acacias in the 19th century as part of the greening of Madrid's southern approaches. The neighbourhood developed around the Rastro flea market area and the old slaughterhouse (Matadero). The station opened in 1968 on Line 5 and serves the transition zone between Arganzuela and the La Latina marketplace district.

name: Marques de Vadillo
etymology_summary: Named after Francisco Antonio de Salcedo y Aguirre (c.1660-1729), 1st Marques de Vadillo, the corregidor (chief magistrate) of Madrid who commissioned the Puente de Toledo bridge. The bridge, designed by Pedro de Ribera in elaborate Churrigueresque style and completed in 1732, was built to improve access across the Manzanares River to the roads leading south toward Toledo. Vadillo's magistracy (1715-1729) was one of the most transformative periods for Madrid's infrastructure. The station sits on Line 5 in the Carabanchel district.
named_after: Francisco Antonio de Salcedo y Aguirre

name: Conde de Casal
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel Escriva de Romani y de la Quintana (1871-1954), Count of Casal, a lawyer, politician, senator, and ceramics historian. He served in the Madrid city council and was a prominent figure in the Restoration-era political establishment. His most lasting contribution was as a historian of Spanish ceramics, producing scholarly works that remain references in the field. The station, on Line 6, serves the Retiro district near the intersection of Calle del Doctor Esquerdo and Calle de Ibiza.

name: Sainz de Baranda
etymology_summary: Named after Pedro Sainz de Baranda y Gorriti (1775-1855), considered Madrid's first constitutional mayor (alcalde constitucional). He led the city government during the tumultuous periods of the War of Independence and the Liberal Triennium (1820-1823). A jurist by training, he championed municipal reform and citizen rights at a time when Spain oscillated between absolutism and liberalism. The station, opened in 1979, is a key interchange between Lines 6 and 9 in the Retiro district.

name: Serrano
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Serrano, honouring Francisco Serrano y Dominguez (1810-1885), who lived and died at number 14. As co-leader of the 1868 Glorious Revolution that overthrew Queen Isabel II, he became regent during the Sexenio Democratico and presided over Spain's first liberal constitution since 1812. The street was named after him following the revolution. Today it is Madrid's most exclusive shopping thoroughfare, the heart of the 'Golden Mile' in the Salamanca district.

name: Velazquez
etymology_summary: Named after Diego Velazquez (1599-1660), court painter to Philip IV and creator of 'Las Meninas', often called the most important painting in Western art. The king appointed him at just 24 and would sit in his studio watching him work, a rare intimacy in the rigid Habsburg court. After Velazquez died, Philip IV wrote 'I am crushed' in the margin of a memorandum. The red cross of Santiago on the painter's chest in Las Meninas was added posthumously — legend says by the king's own hand.

name: Lista
etymology_summary: Named after Alberto Lista y Aragon (1775-1848), a mathematician, poet, journalist, and literary critic from Seville. He was one of the most influential educators of early 19th-century Spain, running schools that shaped a generation of writers including Becquer, Espronceda, and Ventura de la Vega. Although the original street was renamed Calle Jose Ortega y Gasset in 1955, the metro station retained the older name. This makes it one of several Madrid stations whose name no longer matches the street above.

name: Colon
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Colon, honouring Christopher Columbus (Cristobal Colon in Spanish). The plaza features a 17-metre marble monument (1885) by Jeronimo Sunol, with bronze reliefs depicting scenes from the Discovery. In 1977, the underground Centro Cultural de la Villa (now Fernán Gómez Centro Cultural de la Villa) was built beneath the plaza. The nearby Jardines del Descubrimiento (Discovery Gardens) contain massive stone blocks inscribed with quotes from Columbus's diary. The station has served Lines 4 and 8 since its opening in 1944 and 1998 respectively.

name: Republica Argentina
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de la Republica Argentina in the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood of Chamartin, where every street bears the name of a Latin American country or capital. Laid out during mid-20th-century urban expansion, the barrio features Paseo de La Habana, Calle de Chile, Calle Colombia, and plazas honouring Lima, Cuzco, and Ecuador -- a cartographic tribute to Spain's historical ties with the Americas embedded in the very grid of the district.

name: Alonso Cano
etymology_summary: Named after Alonso Cano (1601-1667), a Granadan painter, sculptor, and architect dubbed the 'Spanish Michelangelo' for his mastery of all three arts. A student of Francisco Pacheco alongside Velazquez in Seville, his life took a dark turn in 1644 when his wife was found stabbed to death. Cano was arrested and tortured -- though by royal order his painting hand was spared -- but was exonerated. He later took holy orders in 1658, becoming a canon of Granada Cathedral.

name: Cuzco
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Cuzco, a roundabout on the Paseo de la Castellana that has borne the name of the Peruvian city of Cusco since 21 October 1953. Cusco was the historic capital of the Inca Empire, known as the 'navel of the world' (Qusqu in Quechua). The plaza sits in the Hispanoamerica neighbourhood, part of a cluster of Latin American-themed street names honouring Spain's historical ties to the Americas. It was created in the 1930s following the demolition of the Hipodromo de la Castellana, as part of the northward extension of the Castellana that added five new plazas along a 5 km axis. Today the plaza is a major business hub flanked by corporate towers.

name: Plaza de Castilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Castilla, a major square at the northern end of Paseo de la Castellana honouring the historical Crown of Castile. The plaza is dominated by the Torres Kio (officially Puerta de Europa), two 115-metre inclined towers designed by Philip Johnson and John Burgee, completed in 1996 -- the world's first leaning skyscrapers. The square serves as the northern gateway of Madrid's financial axis and is a major transport interchange. The station, opened in 1961, now connects three Metro lines (1, 9, 10).

name: Alvarado
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Alvarado, honouring Pedro de Alvarado (c.1485-1541), a Spanish conquistador and captain under Hernan Cortes during the conquest of Mexico. Known as 'Tonatiuh' (the Sun) by the Aztecs for his golden hair, Alvarado led the brutal Massacre of the Templo Mayor in 1520 and later conquered Guatemala and El Salvador. His death came when he was crushed by a horse during a failed campaign in Jalisco. The street runs through the Tetuan district in northern Madrid.

name: Puente de Vallecas
etymology_summary: Named after the Puente de Vallecas district, which takes its name from the 18th-century bridge over the Arroyo Abronigal designed by architect Pedro de Ribera around 1731, built in masonry for 65,000 reales. The stream, documented since 1206 watering lands of the Order of Calatrava, once marked the boundary between Madrid and the independent town of Vallecas. Today the Abronigal is buried beneath the M-30 motorway, but the bridge's name endures.

name: Nueva Numancia
etymology_summary: Named after the Nueva Numancia neighbourhood. In 1873, during Spain's First Republic, Don Cayetano Agusti y Giner petitioned the provincial government to declare the area an independent town named after Numancia, the Celtiberian city whose residents chose mass suicide over surrender to Rome in 133 BC. The petition, published in the Boletin Oficial on 15 September 1873, was denied -- yet the defiant name stuck, immortalising the ancient symbol of resistance.

name: Portazgo
etymology_summary: Named after the local area, which references a medieval 'portazgo' -- a toll levied on travellers and merchants for passage through a designated point on a royal road. This particular portazgo stood on the Camino Real de Valencia where it crossed the village of Vallecas, collecting duties on goods entering Madrid from the southeast. Portazgos were granted by the Crown to municipalities or lords as a revenue privilege, and pilgrims were typically exempt. The practice survived into the 18th century, when the Bourbon road reforms gradually replaced tolls with state-funded maintenance.

name: Puerta del Angel
etymology_summary: Named after the Puerta del Angel neighbourhood. On 2 September 1582, festive illuminations ordered by corregidor Luis Gaytan de Ayala to celebrate Felipe II's victory over the Portuguese pretender set the Puerta de Guadalajara -- Madrid's grandest medieval gate -- ablaze, destroying it completely. An angel figure from a niche in the ruined gate was salvaged, and in 1605 the brotherhood of porters of the Casa de Campo built the Ermita del Santo Angel de la Guarda near the Segovian bridge to house it. The neighbourhood that grew up around this chapel entrance to the Casa de Campo has carried the name Puerta del Angel ever since.

name: Alto de Extremadura
etymology_summary: Named after its elevated location ('alto') along the Paseo de Extremadura, the historic road from Madrid toward Badajoz and the Portuguese border. The route descends from the Puerta del Angel, crosses the Manzanares and climbs this hill before heading west. It overlaps with Spain's ancient vias pecuarias, the royal droving trails along which millions of Merino sheep were driven between summer and winter pastures from the 13th century onward under the protection of the Mesta. The territory around the paseo belonged to the municipalities of Carabanchel Alto and Bajo until their annexation to Madrid in 1948.

name: Lucero
etymology_summary: Named after the Lucero neighbourhood in the Latina district. 'Lucero' means 'bright star' or 'morning star' in Spanish, from Latin 'lucifer' (light-bearer). The name's origin as a neighbourhood toponym is undocumented -- it may reference a finca, a person, or a celestial observation point on the elevated terrain of western Madrid. The neighbourhood consolidated after the Civil War as part of the rapid urbanization of the Latina district, which sprawled along the Paseo de Extremadura corridor.

name: Laguna
etymology_summary: Named after the Laguna neighbourhood in the Latina district. 'Laguna' means 'lagoon' or 'small lake' (from Latin lacuna), referencing a former body of standing water that existed in this low-lying area before urbanization. The Latina district historically had several streams (arroyos) tributary to the Manzanares -- Luche, Cano Roto -- now channelled underground. The area's transformation from wetland to dense urban housing occurred mainly in the 1950s-1960s.

name: Aluche
etymology_summary: Named after the Aluche neighbourhood, whose name derives from the Arroyo de Luche, a tributary of the Manzanares that watered extensive orchards in the area. A 1580 Royal Decree of Felipe II already mentions the stream by name when delimiting royal hunting grounds: 'going up said Arroyo, until reaching the land that they call the exido of Aluche'. Early cartographers abbreviated the stream as 'A. Luche' (Arroyo Luche), and over time the abbreviation fused into a single toponym. The stream now flows underground beneath Parque Aluche, where an artificial channel recalls its course. Many of the neighbourhood's streets are named after towns in the province of Toledo, reflecting the origin of migrants who settled here.

name: Campamento
etymology_summary: Named after the Campamento neighbourhood, which references the military camps ('campamentos') established in the area. The name dates to 1885 when the mayor of Carabanchel Alto designated a barrio administrator for 'el barrio de Campamento', acknowledging the military presence. From 1856, during Isabel II's reign, these elevated lands west of Madrid were used for troop manoeuvres and training exercises. Gunpowder was stored here from the late 18th century, and the first barracks were built in the late 1800s. By 1930, roughly half of Carabanchel Alto's population was connected to the military.

name: Batan
etymology_summary: Named after the Venta del Batan in the Casa de Campo. 'Batan' comes from Hispano-Arabic 'battan' (fulling mill), a water-driven device whose hammers beat and thickened woollen cloth. A 1734 royal purchase document describes 'a batan house with stables, a well and a workshop, formerly a flour mill and later a chamois-leather factory' on this site. The present complex was designed by architect Manuel Herrero de Palacios as bull pens for Madrid's San Isidro feria and inaugurated on 11 May 1950. It houses the bulls destined for Las Ventas in the days before each corrida, and aficionados still visit to inspect the animals.

name: Lago
etymology_summary: Named after the lake ('lago') in the Casa de Campo park, a large artificial lake created in the 18th century near the main entrance to Madrid's largest public park. The Casa de Campo, originally a royal hunting estate acquired by Felipe II in 1562, spans 1,722 hectares. The lake became a popular recreation area after the park was opened to the public during the Second Republic in 1931. The station, opened in 1961, serves as a gateway to the park's western zone including the Teleferico cable car.
named_after: Lago de la Casa de Campo (lake)

name: Casa de Campo
etymology_summary: Named after the Casa de Campo, Madrid's largest public park at 1,722 hectares -- five times the size of Central Park in New York. Originally a royal hunting estate acquired by Felipe II in 1562 when he moved the court to Madrid, the grounds featured a palace, gardens, and extensive woodland. It remained exclusively royal for nearly four centuries until the Second Republic opened it to the public in 1931. During the Civil War, the park became the western front line of the Battle of Madrid (1936-39), and trenches and bunkers are still visible. Today it houses the Madrid Zoo, the Parque de Atracciones, and the Teleferico cable car.

name: Plaza de Espana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Espana, which occupies the site of the former Cuartel de San Gil, military barracks designed by Sabatini and demolished in 1906-1908. The Cervantes monument was commissioned by Alfonso XIII in 1915 for the 300th anniversary of Don Quixote Part II, though the bronze Quixote and Sancho were not added until the 1960s. A major 2021 renovation buried traffic in a kilometre-long tunnel and unearthed 18th-century vaults of the Godoy Palace.

name: Ciudad Universitaria
etymology_summary: Named after Madrid's Ciudad Universitaria (University City), home to the Universidad Complutense de Madrid, the Polytechnic University, and UNED. The campus was planned in the 1920s under Alfonso XIII.

name: Pio XII
etymology_summary: Named after Pope Pius XII (Eugenio Pacelli, 1876-1958), who led the Catholic Church through World War II and its aftermath. Elected in a single-day conclave in 1939, his pontificate remains one of the most debated in modern history: defenders credit Vatican networks with saving thousands of Jewish lives, while critics fault his public silence on the Holocaust. The Madrid avenue and station reflect Franco-era Spain's close ties to the Holy See.

name: Duque de Pastrana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza Duque de Pastrana. The Duchy of Pastrana was created in 1572 by Felipe II for his closest confidant, Ruy Gomez de Silva (1516-1573), a Portuguese nobleman who arrived in Castile as a child page in the entourage of Empress Isabel in 1526. Their lifelong bond made Ruy the most influential courtier in Spain, leader of the 'ebolista' faction favouring diplomacy over the Duke of Alba's militarism. His wife was the legendary one-eyed Ana de Mendoza, Princess of Eboli, whom Felipe II imprisoned in Pastrana's ducal palace from 1581 until her death in 1592. The couple also invited Teresa of Avila to found two Discalced Carmelite convents in Pastrana.
named_after: Ruy Gomez de Silva (1st Duke of Pastrana)

name: Herrera Oria
etymology_summary: Named after Angel Herrera Oria (1886-1968), journalist, Catholic social activist, educator, and ultimately a cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church. The thirteenth of fifteen children, he purchased the newspaper El Debate in 1911 and transformed it into one of Spain's most widely read dailies. In 1926 he founded Spain's first school of journalism, attached to the paper. He also created the Asociacion Catolica Nacional de Propagandistas, Editorial Catolica, and the Instituto Social Leon XIII to promote Catholic social doctrine. At fifty-three he left journalism for the priesthood, was ordained in Switzerland in 1940, and was appointed Bishop of Malaga in 1947, where he oversaw the construction of 250 schools across the province. Pope Paul VI made him a cardinal in 1965; his cause of canonisation is now open.

name: Barrio del Pilar
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio del Pilar neighbourhood. Contrary to common belief, the neighbourhood was NOT named after the Virgen del Pilar but after Pilar, the wife of developer Jose Banus, who baptised his first solo real estate project with her name as a wedding gift in 1961. The development on former Jesuit lands housed 45,600 inhabitants in 13,872 homes by 1970.

name: Ventilla
etymology_summary: Named after the Ventilla neighbourhood. 'Ventilla' is a diminutive of 'venta' (inn/tavern), referring to a small roadside inn that stood at the exit of the Carretera de Francia. The area belonged to the old municipality of Chamartin de la Rosa and began attracting settlers in the early 1900s, mostly rural migrants seeking factory work. By the 1920s it was a neighbourhood of overcrowded shacks without running water, known locally as a barrio of rag-collectors. When Chamartin de la Rosa was annexed to Madrid in 1948, Ventilla passed to the district of Tetuan and slowly gained paved streets.

name: Mirasierra
etymology_summary: Named after the Mirasierra neighbourhood, meaning 'Mountain View' -- referring to the panoramic views of the Sierra de Guadarrama from its elevated terrain. The colonia originated in a 1927 project by the Sociedad de Casas Baratas for a satellite city of single-family homes arranged around circular plazas. Developer Banus Hermanos S.A. revived the scheme in 1947, siting it on high ground near the Lozoya water-supply canal, and architect Guillermo Diz Florez designed the first 200 houses in 1948. A Partial Plan approved in 1954 by the architects Manuel and Jose Romero Aguirre finally gave the neighbourhood its definitive form. Its north-facing hilltop position offers some of the clearest mountain vistas in Madrid.

name: Arganzuela-Planetario
etymology_summary: Named after the Arganzuela district and the Planetario de Madrid. The planetarium was inaugurated on 29 September 1986 and sits in the Parque Enrique Tierno Galvan, built on former railway land in Legazpi. The park honours Madrid's beloved socialist mayor, who died in January 1986 just months before the planetarium's completion; the park itself opened on 10 May 1987. The planetarium features a 17.5-metre dome with a Zeiss projector and underwent a major refurbishment in 2016-2017. The metro station opened in 2007 and took a double-barrelled name to distinguish it from the existing Legazpi stop and highlight the planetarium as a local landmark.

name: Suanzes
etymology_summary: Named after Juan Antonio Suanzes Fernandez (1891-1977), a naval engineer and childhood friend of Francisco Franco from their days at the Ferrol naval academy. As first president of the Instituto Nacional de Industria (INI) and Minister of Industry, he masterminded Spain's post-war autarkic industrialisation programme. He was posthumously honoured with the title Marquis of Suanzes in 1960.

name: Ciudad Lineal
etymology_summary: Named after the Ciudad Lineal district, which takes its name from Arturo Soria y Mata's pioneering 'Linear City' urban planning concept (1892-1911). Soria envisioned a narrow city stretching 50 kilometres along a single transportation axis with a central boulevard, electric tram, and individual houses with gardens. Though only 5 km were built before his death in 1920, the idea influenced urban planning worldwide. The Calle de Arturo Soria, a 15 km boulevard, remains the spine of the district.

name: Quintana
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Quintana in Ciudad Lineal, likely honouring Manuel Jose Quintana (1772-1857), the Neoclassical poet crowned national poet by Queen Isabella II in an unprecedented 1855 ceremony. Quintana also served as royal tutor and director of public instruction. The word 'quintana' derives from Latin, originally meaning the market square of a Roman camp, later evolving to denote a village plaza.

name: El Carmen
etymology_summary: Named after the Capilla del Carmen (1928), a chapel at Carretera de Aragon 40 (now C/Alcala 246) run by the Congregacion de las Damas Apostolicas. It served the poor neighbourhoods east of the Abronigal stream. The chapel became the nucleus of the Parroquia Espiritu Santo (1940). Nothing remains except the memory in the station name.

name: Garcia Noblejas
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de los Hermanos Garcia Noblejas, honouring a family of Falangist sympathisers from Manzanares (Ciudad Real) who died during the Spanish Civil War and its aftermath. The father, Salvador Garcia Noblejas y Quesada, was killed at Paracuellos del Jarama in November 1936; Jose fell at the Cuartel de la Montana on 20 July 1936; Jesus was killed at the Battle of Brunete; and Javier died fighting with the Division Azul in Russia in 1941. In 2017, under Mayor Manuela Carmena, the street was renamed Avenida de la Institucion Libre de Ensenanza under Spain's Historical Memory Law, but Madrid's High Court annulled the change, ruling that the brothers held no political or military positions of responsibility. The metro station has retained the original name throughout.

name: Simancas
etymology_summary: Named after the Simancas neighbourhood, which references the Castilian town of Simancas (Valladolid). In 939, King Ramiro II of Leon defeated the Cordoban caliph Abd al-Rahman III at the Battle of Simancas, a decisive Reconquista victory. Legend holds that the town's name recalls the 'Tribute of the Seven Maidens' -- seven women who cut off their own hands rather than be surrendered to the Moors ('si mancas').
