In 1563 Felipe II converted the town's castle into the Archivo General de Simancas, now housing over 33 million documents of state and one of Europe's most important historical archives.

name: Las Musas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Musas neighbourhood, referencing the Muses of Greek mythology. The area was a residential colony (colonia) in the Canillejas zone with mythological and classical street names.

name: San Blas
etymology_summary: Named after the San Blas neighbourhood. Sources indicate it was named as a tribute to Blas Perez Gonzalez (1898-1978), Minister of Gobernacion (Interior) 1942-1957, who oversaw housing policy. The neighbourhood was planned in 1958 under the Obra Sindical del Hogar. The 'San' prefix was added to the minister's first name. The saint association is secondary.

name: Pueblo Nuevo
etymology_summary: Named after the Pueblo Nuevo neighbourhood, meaning 'New Town'. The area originated around 1860 as the Colonia Agricola de la Purisima Concepcion, an agricultural cooperative founded at the junction of Calle de Alcala and the old Aragon highway to supply Madrid's markets with vegetables. Early references called it 'Pueblo Nuevo de la Concepcion', shortened to Pueblo Nuevo by 1925. It straddled the municipalities of Canillas, Canillejas, and Vicalvaro until annexation in 1951.

name: Pinar del Rey
etymology_summary: Named after the Pinar del Rey neighbourhood, meaning 'King's Pine Grove'. The name references a historical royal pine forest that belonged to the Crown in the Hortaleza district, part of the extensive woodland that once covered northern Madrid. The area was gradually urbanized from the 1960s onward, though patches of pine trees survive in local parks. The neighbourhood is part of the broader Hortaleza district, itself an ancient village annexed to Madrid in 1950.

name: Bambú
etymology_summary: Named after Calle Bambu in the Castilla neighbourhood of Chamartin, part of a cluster of streets bearing tropical-plant names -- including Calle Yuca at the very intersection above the station. The botanical naming theme, applied when this area was developed in the mid-20th century, lends an exotic touch to a district once covered by the pine groves and farmland of old Chamartin de la Rosa. The station opened in 2007 on Line 4's northern extension.

name: Estrella
etymology_summary: Named after the Estrella neighbourhood in the Retiro district. The area takes its name from the Calle Estrella (Star Street), part of a neighbourhood that developed in the 19th century along the eastern edge of the Retiro park. The station is located beneath the M-30 motorway near the Avenida del Mediterraneo. The Retiro district, anchored by the great park, is one of Madrid's most affluent areas, blending 19th-century bourgeois architecture with green spaces.

name: Vinateros
etymology_summary: Named after the Camino de Vinateros, an old dirt road used by wine merchants ('vinateros') who transported wine from the vineyards of Arganda and La Mancha to Madrid. The path appears on an 1862 military map as one of the two principal roads through Moratalaz. Wine arrived by cart and later via the Tren de Arganda railway. Over 32 municipalities in the D.O. Vinos de Madrid Subzona de Arganda supplied Madrid through this route. The name preserves the memory of centuries of wine trade that shaped this area's identity.

name: Artilleros
etymology_summary: Named after the Pico de Artilleros, referencing the artillery firing range (campo de tiro de artilleria) established in the dehesa of Moratalaz from 1861. Military exercises ceased after 1927. Troops accessed the range from Calle Granada in Pacifico.

name: Avenida de America
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de America, a major avenue honouring the Americas and the historical ties between Spain and Latin America. The station, opened in 1973, is one of Madrid's most important transport hubs, connecting four metro lines (4, 6, 7, 9) with a major intercity bus terminal serving routes across Spain. The surrounding Hispanoamerica neighbourhood features streets named after Latin American countries and cities, reflecting Spain's deep cultural connections to the continent.

name: Cartagena
etymology_summary: Named after Calle de Cartagena, which references the port city of Cartagena in Murcia, founded as Qart Hadasht ('New City') by the Carthaginian general Hasdrubal in 227 BCE, later becoming the Roman Carthago Nova. The Madrid street runs through the Salamanca and Ciudad Lineal districts; in the 1960s it was extended, absorbing part of Calle Gomez Ortega. The station opened in 1975 on Line 7, serving the eastern edge of the Salamanca grid.

name: Antonio Machado
etymology_summary: Named after Antonio Machado (1875-1939), one of Spain's greatest poets of the Generation of '98. His masterpiece 'Campos de Castilla' (1912), a lyrical meditation on the stark beauty and spiritual decay of the Castilian landscape, was published weeks before the death of his young wife Leonor. He championed what he called 'eternal poetry', rooted in intuition over ornament. A staunch defender of the Republic, Machado fled Spain in January 1939 as Catalonia fell, and died of pneumonia on 22 February 1939 in a modest hotel in Collioure, France; his mother Ana Ruiz died three days later in the same town.

name: Valdezarza
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdezarza neighbourhood in the Moncloa-Aravaca district. 'Valdezarza' likely derives from 'valle de zarza' (bramble valley), referencing wild blackberry bushes in the area.

name: Colonia Jardin
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Jardin, a military housing colony built along the Arroyo Meaques in the 1940s-1950s to house armed forces personnel and their families. Inspired by the garden-city movement of Ebenezer Howard, the colony featured individual chalets with gardens, whose size varied according to the tenant's military rank. Residents had to be both military and married to qualify, and they paid nominal rents for life. The area sits on the boundary between Campamento and Pozuelo de Alarcon, near the spot where three postwar military colonies -- Arroyo Meaques, Dehesa del Principe, and Campamento -- transformed former open fields into a leafy suburban enclave.

name: Opanel
etymology_summary: Named after the Opanel neighbourhood in Carabanchel, which takes its name from the Arroyo de Opanel, a stream that once flowed through the area before being buried during urbanisation. The stream appears on the Facundo Canada Lopez plano of Carabanchel (1900). The toponym may have pre-Roman hydronymic origins: the prefix 'Op-' could relate to the Indo-European root *up-/*op- meaning 'water/river' found in pre-Roman Hispanic toponymy (Villar Liebana, Palaeohispanica 2002). Villar lists Opaca (Huesca) among parallel forms but does not mention Opanel by name; the connection is typological. Madrid/Carabanchel falls in the voiceless *op- variant zone (West/Toledo region). Station opened as 'Elvas' 7 May 1981; renamed 'Opanel' 27 June 1984 at residents' request.
source: Villar Liebana, 'Los hidronimos con *up- (*op-) agua, rio', Palaeohispanica 2 (2002) pp. 277-291 (dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=670065); Plano Facundo Canada Lopez 1900 (digital.csic.es/handle/10261/28971); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Opanel; karabanchel.com

name: Rivas Vaciamadrid
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of Rivas-Vaciamadrid, a composite of two historic settlements. 'Rivas' traces to Guillermo de Ribas, a Segovian captain who founded the town around 1100 at the initiative of the Council of Segovia. 'Vaciamadrid' derives from Arabic 'Fahs al-Mayrit' (field of Madrid), referring to agricultural lands that supplied Muslim-era Madinat al-Mayrit. The Arabist Jaime Oliver Asin documented the name's evolution through medieval forms: 'Ahazalmadrit', 'Mazalmadrit', 'Macal Madrit', and finally 'Vaciamadrid'. Both towns were destroyed during the Civil War, lying directly on the front line, and were rebuilt as a single nucleus by the General Directorate of Devastated Regions in 1954.

name: Julian Besteiro
etymology_summary: Named after Julian Besteiro Fernandez (1870-1940), a university professor and socialist politician. He served as president of the Spanish Parliament (Cortes Constituyentes) from 1931-1933 during the Second Republic, and was president of both the PSOE and UGT. Educated at the Institucion Libre de Ensenanza and the Sorbonne, he led the moderate wing of Spanish socialism. He died in Carmona prison after being sentenced by a Francoist court martial.

name: Juan de la Cierva
etymology_summary: Named after Juan de la Cierva y Codorniu (1895-1936), the Spanish civil engineer and aviator from Murcia who invented the autogiro (autogyro), the precursor to the modern helicopter. His C.4 prototype achieved the first successful flight of a stable rotary-wing aircraft in 1923. He died in a KLM plane crash at Croydon Airport, London.

name: Alonso de Mendoza
etymology_summary: Named after Alonso de Mendoza y Nunez de Prado (d. c. 1507), a steward (mayordomo) of Archbishop Alfonso Carrillo de Albornoz who served as mayor of Bonilla de la Sierra. In his 1507 will, he bequeathed nearly all his assets to found the Hospital de San Jose in Getafe, one of Spain's oldest continuously operating charitable foundations, serving the poor of Getafe, Pinto, and Grinon.
named_after: Alonso de Mendoza y Nunez de Prado

name: Hospital Severo Ochoa
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario Severo Ochoa in Leganes, which is itself named after Severo Ochoa de Albornoz (1905-1993), the Asturian biochemist who won the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering the enzymes involved in RNA synthesis. The hospital's construction began in 1981, opened partially in 1987, and was officially inaugurated in 1988 with Severo Ochoa himself attending.

name: Reyes Catolicos
etymology_summary: Named after the Reyes Catolicos (Catholic Monarchs): Queen Isabella I of Castile (1451-1504) and King Ferdinand II of Aragon (1452-1516), whose marriage unified the crowns of Castile and Aragon. The station is in San Sebastian de los Reyes, a town the monarchs themselves founded: on 2 May 1492, they signed a Royal Decree ordering the Council of Madrid to establish a settlement for thirty-two families fleeing feudal abuses in neighbouring Alcobendas. The refugees had gathered near a hermitage of San Sebastian on royal-domain land, deliberately choosing Crown territory over seigneurial control. That same year the monarchs completed the Reconquista and dispatched Columbus westward.
named_after: Reyes Catolicos (Isabella I and Ferdinand II)

name: Manuel de Falla
etymology_summary: Named after Manuel de Falla (1876-1946), one of Spain's greatest classical composers. His ballet 'El Sombrero de Tres Picos' (1919), with sets and costumes by Picasso and choreography for Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, became a worldwide sensation at its London premiere. Other masterworks include 'El Amor Brujo' (1915) and 'Noches en los Jardines de Espana' (1916). A painful eye disease, recurrent acute iridocyclitis, progressively impaired his vision and shaped his reclusive later years. After the Civil War he refused Franco's pension, left for Argentina in 1939, and died in Alta Gracia in 1946 leaving his vast cantata 'Atlantida' unfinished.

name: Marqués de la Valdavia
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza Duque de Pastrana. The Marquesado de la Valdavia was created 13 June 1879 by Alfonso XII. First holder: Josefa Lamadrid Cosio. The II Marques, Mariano Osorio de Lamadrid (1851-1898), was deputy for Saldana and senator. The III Marques was President of Madrid's Provincial Delegation (1947-1965). Title derives from the Valdavia river valley in Palencia.
source: es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marquesado_de_la_Valdavia; historiadelascallesdealcobendas.blogspot.com/2009/04/calle-del-marques-de-la-valdavia.html; comunidad.madrid/archivos (fondo Marqueses de la Valdavia); dbe.rah.es

name: Avenida de la Paz
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de la Paz, the eastern section of the M-30 ring road built along the former Abroñigal stream bed. The avenue was inaugurated in 1974 and named in allusion to peace, likely referencing the post-Civil War era. Officially denominated in 1991.
named_after: Avenida de la Paz (M-30 eastern section)

name: San Lorenzo
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de San Lorenzo and its parish. San Lorenzo (Saint Lawrence of Rome, c. 225-258) was born in Huesca, Spain, and served as one of the seven deacons of Rome under Pope Sixtus II. When Emperor Valerian demanded the Church's treasures, Lawrence presented the poor and sick, declaring them 'the true treasures of the Church'. Martyred on a gridiron, he reportedly told his executioners 'Turn me over, I am done on this side'. He is patron saint of cooks, librarians, and firefighters, and third patron of Rome. His feast day, 10 August, gives its name to San Lorenzo de El Escorial.

name: Parque de Santa Maria
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de Santa María neighbourhood in Hortaleza, which takes its name from the Parroquia Santa María del Parque (Parish of Saint Mary of the Park) established in the 1970s. The neighbourhood was built in the 1960s by the developer Construcciones Residenciales y Sociales.

name: Hortaleza
etymology_summary: Named after the district of Hortaleza, a former independent village annexed to Madrid in 1950. The name derives from the Latin 'hortus' (garden/orchard), referring to the abundant vegetable gardens historically cultivated in the area, though some theories suggest it derives from 'fortaleza' (fortress).

name: Manoteras
etymology_summary: Named after the area of Manoteras, first documented in 1807 as 'Las Manoteras'. According to philologist Emilio Nieto Ballester, the name derives from Latin 'lumba altaria' (high hills), evolving through 'Lomaotera' to 'La Manotera', describing the elevated terrain between Fuencarral and Hortaleza.
source: Nieto Ballester 'Breve diccionario de toponimos espanoles' (1997); historias-matritenses.blogspot.com/2015/02/manoteras-o-el-barrio-de-santiago.html; memoriademanoteras.es; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Manoteras

name: Empalme
etymology_summary: Named after the railway junction ('empalme' means junction/connection) between the Madrid-Almorox narrow-gauge line and the Ferrocarril Suburbano de Carabanchel. The Madrid-Almorox line, operating 1891-1965, was a narrow-gauge railway serving the western outskirts. A flag stop called 'Empalme-Goya' was established where the two rail systems crossed, allowing passengers to transfer. The word 'empalme' comes from 'empalmar' (to splice/join), originally a nautical term for joining ropes. The station opened in 1961 on Line 5.

name: Urgel
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Urgel, referencing the Condado de Urgell in Catalonia (Lleida), one of the most powerful medieval Catalan counties. Carved out of the Carolingian March around 798, Urgell became an independent dynasty under Ermengol I in 992 and played a major role in the Reconquista of the Segre valley. The last male heir, Jaume II 'el Dissortat' (the Unlucky), lost his claim to the Crown of Aragon at the Compromise of Caspe in 1412 and died imprisoned in Xativa castle in 1433, ending the county's storied lineage.

name: El Capricho
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de El Capricho, the only surviving romantic garden in Madrid. Created between 1787 and 1839 by Maria Josefa Pimentel (1752-1834), Duchess of Osuna, the estate was her 'capricho' (whim). Goya painted six witchcraft scenes for the palace, including 'El Aquelarre' and 'Vuelo de Brujas', commissioned by the duchess in 1797-98. During the Civil War, General Miaja's Republican Army of the Centre built its headquarters in a 2000 m2 bunker excavated 15 metres beneath the garden; it survives and can be visited today. The park showcases three styles -- French parterre, English landscape, and Italian giardino -- and opens only on weekends.

name: Alameda de Osuna
etymology_summary: Named after the Alameda de Osuna neighbourhood. 'Alameda' means a poplar-lined promenade; 'Osuna' refers to the dukes whose estate dominated this area. The key figure is Maria Josefa Pimentel (1752-1834), XII Countess-Duchess of Benavente, called the 'influencer of the Spanish Enlightenment': first woman admitted to the Royal Economic Society of Madrid, host of the capital's foremost literary salon, and patron of Goya, Moratin, and other artists. Goya painted the family portrait now in the Prado and six witchcraft scenes for the estate. She created the adjacent El Capricho garden as a meeting place for intellectuals. The neighbourhood grew around the ducal grounds after the estate's decline.

name: Pitis
etymology_summary: Named after the Pitis area in Fuencarral-El Pardo district, a pre-existing rural place name documented before the Cercanias station opened on 25 May 1964. The exact origin is genuinely unknown -- the FilobLogos blog on Madrid natural toponymy (2007) explicitly lists Pitis among names for which 'no se saben'. The area was described c.1960 as having 'una frondosa alameda' (leafy poplar grove) with a stream. One speculative hypothesis links it to Greek 'Pitys' (pine), paralleling the Pitiusas islands etymology. Circumstantial support: the 'Arroyo de los Pinos' (Stream of the Pines) flows through the adjacent Penagrande neighbourhood, and the nearby Monte de El Pardo has extensive pine forests. However, no mechanism for a Greek form entering Castilian rural toponymy is established. Alternative: personal name or nickname of a landowner, now lost. No scholarly publication has treated this toponym. A shantytown of ~150 mostly Portuguese families grew around the station until demolition c. 2005.
source: FilobLogos 2007 (filoblogos.blogspot.com/2007/02/toponimia-natural-de-madrid.html); eldiario.es 2021; historias-matritenses.blogspot.com/2010/11/penagrande-lacoma-el-barrio.html; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Pitis; Ayto. Madrid (Parque Arroyo de los Pinos)

name: Arroyofresno
etymology_summary: Named after the Arroyo del Fresno (Ash Tree Stream) residential area. The name combines 'arroyo' (stream) and 'fresno' (ash tree) describing the natural landscape of a stream lined with ash trees that historically flowed through this part of northern Madrid.

name: Lacoma
etymology_summary: Named after Margarita González Lacoma (1896-1976) a Spanish businesswoman from Burgos who founded Casa Lacoma a haute couture fashion house on Gran Vía in 1925. She later became a real estate developer building the Colonia Lacoma workers' housing development in this area in the 1940s-50s.

name: Avenida de la Ilustracion
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de la Ilustracion ('Avenue of the Enlightenment'), referencing the 18th-century intellectual movement that reached its Spanish zenith under Carlos III (1759-1788). Popularly called 'el Mejor Alcalde de Madrid' (the Best Mayor of Madrid), Carlos III found a dirty, poorly lit capital and transformed it: he paved streets, installed public lighting and sewers, built the Cibeles and Neptune fountains, the Puerta de Alcala, and the building that now houses the Prado Museum. His reign also promoted scientific academies and the Economic Societies of Friends of the Country, making Madrid a centre of Enlightenment thought in southern Europe.

name: Peñagrande
etymology_summary: Named after the Peñagrande neighbourhood meaning 'Large Rock'. The name references a prominent large rock formation that for centuries served as a landmark for shepherds and inhabitants of the area. The colony of Peñagrande originated in 1914 as 'Colonia El Porvenir-Fuente la Mina'.

name: Parque de las Avenidas
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de las Avenidas (Park of the Avenues) a park designed by architect Cecilio Rodríguez and built between 1928 and 1933. The name refers to the major avenues that define the surrounding neighbourhood's layout particularly Avenida de Bruselas and other European city-named streets.

name: Barrio de la Concepcion
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de la Concepción which originated as the 'Colonia Agrícola La Purísima Concepción' (Agricultural Colony of the Immaculate Conception) in the 19th century. The name refers to the Catholic dogma of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary later reinforced by the local parish.

name: Ascao
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de Ascao in Pueblo Nuevo, Ciudad Lineal. The street name derives from Ascao/Askao, a historic neighbourhood in Bilbao's Old Town (Casco Viejo). The Madrid street follows a Basque-origin naming pattern: the adjacent Barrio de Bilbao was founded by a wealthy Basque family, and its streets were named after places in the province of Vizcaya. The Basque toponym 'Askao' is composed of 'aska' (manger/watering trough/ditch) + 'ao' (mouth), referring to the horseshoe shape of the Bilbao estuary.
source: Aunamendi Eusko Entziklopedia (aunamendi.eusko-ikaskuntza.eus/es/ascao/ar-15357); Irigoien etymology; Guiard 'Historia de la villa de Bilbao'; deia.eus/contando-historias/2024/02/25/calle-askao; nosolometro.blogspot.com; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pueblo_Nuevo_(Ciudad_Lineal)

name: Barrio del Puerto
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio del Puerto neighbourhood in Coslada. The name references the nearby Puerto Seco (Dry Port) de Coslada a major inland logistics platform established in 1995-2001 that connects with Spain's four largest seaports.

name: Coslada Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Coslada municipality. 'Coslada' has disputed etymology: possibly from Latin 'cos' (flint) + 'late' (abundant) or from Celtic 'coslo/cosla' (hazelnut) or from Latin 'cova ustulata' (burnt cave). The town dates back to at least 1083.

name: La Rambla
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de la Rambla in Coslada. 'Rambla' derives from Arabic 'ramla' (sand), denoting a dry riverbed that only carries water after heavy rains. In the landscape a rambla is a wide, flat-bottomed channel with steep banks and a substrate of gravel and sand, common across Mediterranean Spain. Barcelona's famous Rambla was literally an intermittent stream until 1440, when the watercourse was diverted and the dry bed became a promenade. In Coslada the name preserves the memory of seasonal watercourses that once drained toward the Henares river across otherwise arid terrain.
named_after: La Rambla neighbourhood (Coslada, from Arabic ramla: sandy riverbed)

name: San Fernando
etymology_summary: Named after the municipality of San Fernando de Henares which honours Saint Ferdinand III of Castile (1199-1252). King Fernando VI who founded the town's Real Fábrica de Paños (Royal Cloth Factory) in the 1740s named it after his patron saint Ferdinand III canonized in 1671.

name: Jarama
etymology_summary: Named after the nearby Jarama River the longest and most voluminous river crossing the Madrid region. The river name has disputed origins: possibly from an Indo-European root *sar- (to flow) modified during Islamic rule; or from Berber meaning 'border river'; or from 'jara' (rockrose shrub).

name: Henares
etymology_summary: Named after the Henares River near whose course the station is located. The name derives from Spanish 'henar' (field of hay/heno) the plural form describing the hay fields historically cultivated along the river's banks. The river was known as Guadalajara during Arab rule.

name: Hospital del Henares
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario del Henares, a public hospital in Coslada that opened simultaneously with the metro station in February 2008. The hospital serves the rapidly growing Corredor del Henares population. It is named after the Henares River, whose name derives from Spanish 'henar' (hay field), the plural form describing the hay meadows historically cultivated along its banks. The river was known as 'Guadalajara' during Arab rule, meaning 'valley/river of stones'. The station is on Line 7's MetroEste extension.

name: Buenos Aires
etymology_summary: Named after Avenida de Buenos Aires, part of a Latin American-themed street cluster in Vallecas. The name traces back to at least 1880, when an 'Alto de Buenos Aires' hilltop was documented. The current avenue was formally laid out in 1968-1971 as Vallecas urbanised rapidly. Surrounding streets reference other Spanish-American capitals, reflecting Madrid's practice of honouring its historic ties to Latin America through neighbourhood-scale thematic naming.

name: Alto del Arenal
etymology_summary: Named after the Alto del Arenal neighbourhood in Entrevias. 'Alto' means high ground; 'arenal' means sandy terrain, describing the elevated sandy bluffs east of Vallecas. During the 1950s, massive rural-to-urban migration created a severe housing crisis in Madrid: by 1956 the Entrevias sector alone had over 4,300 shacks (chabolas). The Franco regime responded with 'poblados dirigidos' (directed settlements) to replace the informal housing, transforming Entrevias and Alto del Arenal into planned working-class neighbourhoods. The station opened only in 2007 on Line 1, finally connecting this long-underserved area to the metro network.

name: Miguel Hernandez
etymology_summary: Named after the street honouring Miguel Hernandez Gilabert (1910-1942), one of Spain's greatest 20th-century poets. Associated with the Generation of '36, he died in a Francoist prison of tuberculosis. Author of 'El rayo que no cesa' and 'Viento del pueblo'.

name: Sierra de Guadalupe
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle Sierra de Guadalupe, referencing the Sierra de Guadalupe mountain range in Extremadura (Caceres). At the foot of these mountains sits the Royal Monastery of Santa Maria de Guadalupe, founded in the 14th century after a shepherd reportedly discovered a hidden statue of the Virgin near the Guadalupe river. King Alfonso XI attributed his 1340 victory at the Battle of Rio Salado to the Virgin's intercession and made it a royal sanctuary. Entrusted to the Hieronymites in 1389, the monastery became one of Spain's richest; Columbus made his first pilgrimage here after discovering America in 1492. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 1993, recognising four centuries of religious architecture spanning Gothic, Mudejar, and Renaissance styles.

name: Villa de Vallecas
etymology_summary: Named after the historic Villa de Vallecas, independent until annexed by Madrid in 1950. 'Vallecas' etymology is genuinely debated: Federico Corriente proposes Arabic 'ballaykás' (zones of valley) from Latin 'vallis' with Arabic suffix -- the most favoured scholarly theory. Alternatives include 'Vallis Egas' (valley of a person named Egas) per Pellicer (1803), and the folk legend of an Arab named 'Kas'. First documented in the 1202 Fuero de Madrid as 'Balecas'. The Cerro de la Gavia nearby holds an Iron Age Carpetano settlement from the 4th century BC.

name: Congosto
etymology_summary: Named after the surrounding neighbourhood. 'Congosto' derives from Latin 'coangustus' (narrow/constricted), meaning a gorge or narrow pass between terrain features. The prefix 'co-' (together) with 'angustus' (narrow) evokes two terrain elements closing to create a tight passage. A frequent toponym across Spain for narrow river gorges or defile passages, historically exploited for mills and water infrastructure.

name: La Gavia
etymology_summary: Named after the Arroyo de La Gavia, a tributary of the Manzanares flowing through Villa de Vallecas. 'Gavia' derives from Latin 'cavea' (cavity), meaning a drainage ditch or trench dug in the earth. The Cerro de La Gavia is an important archaeological site with occupations from the Paleolithic through the Iron Age Carpetano settlement (4th century BC) to Late Antiquity. The Carpetanos chose this defensive position between ravines near the stream confluence.
named_after: Arroyo de La Gavia (from Latin cavea, drainage ditch)
source: RAE; iedra.es/palabras/gavia; GIPL (parquelineal.es/historia/carpetanos/poblado-de-la-gavia); Morin de Pablos et al. (dialnet.unirioja.es/servlet/articulo?codigo=6576968); Complutum UCM (revistas.ucm.es/index.php/CMPL/article/view/58481)

name: Valdecarros
etymology_summary: Named after the Valdecarros area in Villa de Vallecas. Traditionally interpreted as 'Valle de Carros' (Valley of Carts), referring to the route through this valley used by merchandise carts. An alternative theory derives it from 'Valle de Navarros' (Valley of the Navarrese), referring to Navarrese resettlers granted land here during the late 12th-century Reconquista repopulation campaigns. A parallel toponym Valdecarros exists in Salamanca province (also founded during medieval repopulation), strengthening the Navarrese theory. Earliest documented mention: 21 April 1296, in a purchase and sale document. Part of a rich cluster of Val(de)- toponyms in Vallecas: Valdeculebras, Valderribas, Valdemingomez, Valdeolmos.
named_after: Valdecarros (Valley of Carts or Valley of the Navarrese)

name: Las Rosas
etymology_summary: Named after the Las Rosas neighbourhood. 'Las Rosas' (The Roses) likely references a former estate or garden with rose bushes. The neighbourhood developed rapidly from the 1980s as part of Madrid's eastern expansion.

name: Avenida de Guadalajara
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Guadalajara, the major road leading northeast toward the city of Guadalajara. The name derives from Arabic 'Wadi al-Hijara' (valley of stones), referring to the gravelly bed of the Henares river. Under Muslim rule Guadalajara was governed by the Berber Banu Salim clan as part of the Middle March of al-Andalus, until Alfonso VI annexed it peacefully in 1085 with the fall of the Taifa of Toledo. The city's landmark is the Palacio del Infantado, a 15th-century Gothic-Mudejar masterpiece built by the Mendoza family; it was severely damaged by Nationalist bombing on 6 December 1936 during the Civil War and was painstakingly restored from 1961.

name: Alsacia
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza de Alsacia (Alsace Square), part of a cluster of European geography-themed street names in the San Blas-Canillejas district. Alsace, the Rhine-frontier region between France and Germany, has been one of Europe's most contested territories: French from 1648 (Peace of Westphalia), annexed by Germany in 1871 after the Franco-Prussian War, returned to France in 1919, seized again by the Nazis in 1940, and definitively French once more in 1945. Its four changes of sovereignty in 75 years made Alsace a symbol of Franco-German rivalry and, ultimately, of European reconciliation -- a fitting emblem for a neighbourhood whose streets celebrate the continent's shared geography.

name: La Almudena
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de la Almudena, referencing the Virgen de la Almudena, patron saint of Madrid. 'Almudena' derives from Arabic 'al-mudayna' (the small citadel/walled enclosure). According to tradition, when Muslim forces captured Madrid in 712, Christians hid the statue of the Virgin inside a niche in the city ramparts to save it from destruction. When Alfonso VI reconquered Madrid in 1085, soldiers prayed for guidance and a section of the wall crumbled to reveal the image -- reportedly still flanked by burning candles after more than 300 years. The present statue dates to c. 1500 and is attributed to the Netherlandish sculptor Diego Copin de Holanda. Her feast day, 9 November, is a major holiday in Madrid and the cathedral bears her name.

name: La Elipa
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de la Elipa. The name derives from 'Phelipa' or 'Felipa', referring to Phelipa de Vargas, a 13th-century noblewoman who owned lands in this area east of Madrid. Over centuries, 'tierra de la Phelipa' was shortened and corrupted to 'la Elipa'. This etymology is documented in historical land records and supported by Madrid toponymy scholars including Aparisi Laporta.
source: Aparisi Laporta, Toponimia madrilena (2001); madridnofrills.com; research on medieval land records

name: San Fermin-Orcasur
etymology_summary: 'San Fermin' named by Federico Mayo Gayarre, Navarran businessman and first director of the Instituto Nacional de la Vivienda, who in 1941 named the colony after San Fermin (patron of Navarra) with Navarrese street names (Estafeta, Elizondo). 'Orcasur' = Orcasitas Sur. 'Orcasitas' from the Orcasitas/Horcasitas family of Vizcaya (Basque *horkatz*: roe deer), landowners of the farmland where the neighbourhood developed.

name: Ciudad de los Angeles
etymology_summary: Named after the neighbourhood, which was named via a popular contest in 1958 due to its proximity to the Cerro de los Angeles (Hill of the Angels) in Getafe, the geographic and symbolic centre of the Iberian Peninsula. Built in the 1950s-60s as a satellite city for immigrant workers. Streets were named after zarzuelas (Spanish light operas) in 1983.
named_after: Cerro de los Angeles (geographic centre of Iberian Peninsula)

name: Villaverde Bajo-Cruce
etymology_summary: 'Villaverde' = 'green village', from Latin 'villa viridis'. 'Bajo' = 'lower' (vs Alto). 'Cruce' ('crossing') marks the point where the Extremadura and Andalucia-Levante main-line railways bifurcate, making this one of Madrid's oldest and most strategic rail junctions. The first station opened here on 9 February 1861 on the Madrid-Aranjuez corridor; a larger MZA-company replacement designed in 1924 was inaugurated in 1931 with expanded freight yards. A fatal collision between the Andalucia express and the Toledo train at this bifurcation on 11 June 1921 underscored the crossing's complexity. Villaverde was an independent municipality until annexed by Madrid in 1954.
source: Wikipedia; Ayto. Madrid; escritoresvillaverde.wixsite.com/madrid (Historia: Estaciones de tren en Villaverde); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villaverde_Bajo-Cruce_(Madrid_Metro)

name: San Cristobal
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de San Cristobal de los Angeles in Villaverde, honouring Saint Christopher, patron of travellers. The neighbourhood was built between 1958 and 1965 on the site of the former Norah brick factory, whose chimney still stands as a landmark. Designed to house workers drawn by Villaverde's railway-fuelled industrialisation -- begun when the Madrid-Aranjuez line opened in 1851 -- its 5,828 homes were erected in under a decade by a team of eight architects led by Eugenio Casar. Most early residents were internal migrants from Andalusia and Extremadura, and construction problems on the clay soil have plagued the buildings ever since.

name: Villaverde Alto
etymology_summary: 'Villaverde' = 'green village', from Latin 'villa viridis'; 'Alto' = upper, distinguishing the hilltop old town from Villaverde Bajo below. This was the historic centre of the independent municipality of Villaverde, annexed by Madrid in 1954. A major railway junction since the 19th century, Villaverde Alto became one of Madrid's chief industrial zones in the 1950s when Eduardo Barreiros built a vast 1,300,000 m2 truck and engine factory here in 1954, making Barreiros Diesel one of Spain's largest manufacturers. The factory later passed through Chrysler, Peugeot, and Renault hands, anchoring a blue-collar identity that persists in the neighbourhood today.

name: Penagrande
etymology_summary: Named after the Barrio de Penagrande. 'Pena' = rock/crag; 'grande' = large. Describes a prominent large rock formation that characterized this area before urbanization. First documented May 1807 in a Fuencarral land sale listing 'huerta de la peña grande (de 5 fanegas)'. The colony originated in 1914 as 'Colonia El Porvenir-Fuente la Mina'. Area also known as Beacos in earlier references.

name: Aeropuerto T1-T2-T3
etymology_summary: Named after terminals 1, 2, and 3 of Aeropuerto Adolfo Suarez Madrid-Barajas. The airport opened on 22 April 1931 on 330 hectares of barren land near the town of Barajas ('Barajas' possibly from Arabic 'baraya', tower/lookout), replacing the Getafe and Carabanchel military airfields; commercial flights began in 1933. On 24 March 2014, the airport was officially renamed Adolfo Suarez Madrid-Barajas in honour of Spain's first democratic prime minister after the Franco dictatorship, who had died the previous day. Today it is Spain's busiest airport and one of the largest in Europe by passenger volume.

name: Aeropuerto T4
etymology_summary: Named after Terminal 4 of Madrid-Barajas airport, designed by Richard Rogers and Antonio Lamela and opened in February 2006. Its undulating gull-wing roof shelters over 200,000 m2 of gently curved bamboo ceiling slats -- the largest industrial bamboo installation in the world. Natural light floods through roof 'canyons' between the peaks, supported by rainbow-painted steel 'trees' that double as a wayfinding system grading from warm yellow (landside) to cool blue (airside). The design won the 2006 RIBA Stirling Prize, Britain's most prestigious architecture award, and at 760,000 m2 T4 remains one of Europe's largest terminal buildings.

name: Rivas-Urbanizaciones
etymology_summary: Named after the urbanizaciones (housing estates) of Rivas-Vaciamadrid. These planned suburban communities grew rapidly from the 1990s, transforming Rivas from a small agricultural town (population 500 in 1981) to a city of over 90,000. The municipality name combines 'Rivas' (from Guillermo Rivas, an 11th-century military founder) with 'Vaciamadrid' (from Arabic 'Fahs al-Mayrit': field/pasture of Madrid, NOT 'empty Madrid' as folk etymology suggests). The station opened in 1999 on Line 9.

name: Rivas Futura
etymology_summary: Named after the Rivas Futura development in Rivas-Vaciamadrid, a municipality that exploded from 500 inhabitants in the 1980s to over 100,000 -- one of Spain's fastest growth rates. 'Futura' captures the forward-looking vision of this mixed-use project featuring business parks, a 13-screen cinema, and the H2O shopping centre. The station opened in 2006 on Line 9's southeastern extension.

name: Puerta del Sur
etymology_summary: Named 'Puerta del Sur' (Southern Gate) as the station serves as the gateway connecting the Madrid Metro network (Line 10) with the MetroSur circular line. The name reflects its role as the entry point to southern Madrid's metro system from the city center.
source: Metro de Madrid; Wikipedia; alcorcon.org; crtm.es; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Puerta_del_Sur

name: Joaquin Vilumbrales
etymology_summary: Named after Joaquin Vilumbrales Lopez (1941-1999), a physics teacher and director of Instituto Los Castillos in Alcorcon who entered politics in 1982. After twelve years on the city council, he won an absolute majority in 1999 — the first centre-right mayor ever elected in the traditionally left-leaning southern suburbs of Madrid. He served only three months before dying of lymphatic cancer. Both this station and a municipal library honour his memory.

name: Cuatro Vientos
etymology_summary: Named after the Cuatro Vientos area. The toponym ('Four Winds') predates the aerodrome and refers to the geographic characteristic of this open, elevated plain where winds blow from all four cardinal directions. The exposed, flat terrain later made it ideal for aviation: in 1911 a military commission proposed acquiring the lands for Spain's first military aerodrome, birthplace of Spanish aviation.

name: Aviacion Espanola
etymology_summary: Named in homage to the nearby Madrid-Cuatro Vientos Airport, the oldest aerodrome in Spain (founded 1911) and birthplace of Spanish aviation. Key milestones at Cuatro Vientos include the first military aerodrome (1911), first Spanish wind tunnel (1921, by Emilio Herrera), and Herrera's spacesuit prototype (1935) later studied by NASA.
source: Wikipedia; Aviacion Digital; Comunidad de Madrid

name: Begona
etymology_summary: Named after the Colonia Virgen de Begona residential development near Hospital La Paz. The Virgin of Begona is the patroness of Bilbao and Biscay. 'Begona' derives from Basque 'beg-oina' (place at the foot of the hill), referring to the location of the sanctuary in Bilbao. The colony was built in the 1960s to house workers from northern Spain, many of Basque origin, who migrated to Madrid during the industrial boom. The nearby Hospital La Paz (1964) is one of Spain's largest university hospitals.

name: Fuencarral
etymology_summary: Named after the historic town of Fuencarral, from 'fuente' (spring) + 'carral' (cart road): literally 'spring on the cart road'. An independent municipality for centuries, Fuencarral was forcibly annexed to Madrid by decree on 10 November 1950, absorbing 16,377 inhabitants and 54 square kilometres into the capital. During the Civil War the Calle Fuencarral in the city centre was one of the streets most punished by Nationalist artillery, with unexploded shells turning up in demolished buildings decades later. Today the district of Fuencarral-El Pardo, formed in 1987, is Madrid's largest by area.

name: Ronda de la Comunicacion
etymology_summary: Named after the ring road encircling Distrito Telefonica, the corporate campus designed by Rafael de La-Hoz and inaugurated in 2008. Built in 36 months on 370,000 m2 in Las Tablas, the complex consolidated 14,000 employees under a canopy of photovoltaic panels covering 3.8 hectares. Telefonica financed the station's construction; the name 'de la Comunicacion' reflects the campus's original branding before being renamed in 2011.
named_after: Ronda de la Comunicacion (ring road at Telefonica campus)

name: La Granja
etymology_summary: Named after a street in the Vereda del Pobre industrial park of Alcobendas. 'La Granja' means 'the farm', referencing the agricultural origins of this area. The station was originally planned as 'Alcobendas Industrial' but was renamed to La Granja before opening. Alcobendas transformed from an agricultural village to an industrial and commercial hub in the second half of the 20th century, and this station serves the modern business parks that replaced the former farmland. Opened in 2007 on the Line 10 extension.

name: La Moraleja
etymology_summary: Named after the La Moraleja luxury residential area of Alcobendas. 'Moraleja' is a diminutive collective of 'mora' (mulberry), meaning 'place of mulberry trees'. Originally a royal hunting estate under Carlos III.
source: Toponomasticon Hispaniae (toponhisp.org/es/toponimia-de-las-zonas-central-sur-e-insular-atlantica/toponimo/moraleja); lamoraleja.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Moraleja; Ayto. Alcobendas

name: Baunatal
etymology_summary: Named after Baunatal, a town in Hesse, Germany, twin city of San Sebastian de los Reyes since 1990. The twinning gave rise to the Avenida de Baunatal, and the metro station beneath it inherited the name when Line 10 reached the area in 2007. Baunatal owes its prominence to the Volkswagen Kassel plant established there in 1958, now the largest VW components factory in the world, with some 16,500 employees producing half of the group's gearboxes. It is one of the very few Madrid metro stations named after a foreign city, a quirk that often surprises riders.
source: Wikipedia; Ayto. San Sebastian de los Reyes

name: Hospital Infanta Sofia
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario Infanta Sofia in San Sebastian de los Reyes, which honours Infanta Sofia of Spain (born 2007). The station opened on 26 April 2007 as 'Hospital del Norte', part of the MetroNorte extension that pushed Line 10 northward from Fuencarral to serve Alcobendas and San Sebastian de los Reyes. It was renamed Hospital Infanta Sofia on 8 August 2008 after the hospital itself was named for the younger daughter of King Felipe VI. As the northern terminus of Line 10, it is one of the metro system's outermost stations, located well beyond the M-40 ring road.

name: La Fortuna
etymology_summary: Named after the La Fortuna neighbourhood of Leganes, founded in 1960 by developer Domingo dos Santos 'El Portugues'. Dos Santos swapped land he owned in the Madrid shanty-town of Orcasitas for a plot on the Leganes border, and the first 33 families -- evicted from Orcasitas and earning their living from livestock, scrap collection and waste recycling -- became the neighbourhood's pioneers. He named it 'La Fortuna' after his deceased wife Fortunata Gonzalez Arroyo, and christened the first streets with the saints' names of his children and friends. In the early 1980s Leganes paved the streets, built schools and launched bus routes to end the neighbourhood's isolation; in 1993 La Fortuna became one of the Community of Madrid's first decentralised district boards.

name: La Peseta
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de la Peseta, honouring Spain's former national currency. The peseta was introduced on 19 October 1868 as part of the monetary reform following the Glorious Revolution, making Spain one of the first countries to adopt a decimal currency system. 'Peseta' is a Catalan diminutive of 'peso' (piece/weight). The currency circulated for 133 years until it was replaced by the euro on 1 January 2002. When the station opened in 2006, residents of this Carabanchel neighbourhood petitioned for the name 'Salvador Allende' after a nearby street, but the authorities chose La Peseta instead.

name: Carabanchel Alto
etymology_summary: Upper part of the former Carabanchel municipality (annexed by Madrid in 1948). 'Carabanchel' etymology is debated: possibly Celtic 'kar-' (stone) + suffix, or Arabic, or a personal name; 'Alto' = upper. The neighbourhood is indelibly linked to the Carcel de Carabanchel, a panopticon-style prison built with Republican forced labour between 1940 and 1944. Under Franco it held thousands of political prisoners -- socialists, communists, and union leaders -- and was one of the largest prisons in Europe. After the transition to democracy it housed common criminals and ETA members until its closure in 1998 and demolition in 2008.

name: San Francisco
etymology_summary: Named after the Calle de San Francisco, honouring the historic Franciscan presence in the Carabanchel area. Saint Francis of Assisi (c.1181-1226) founded the Franciscan order, which established numerous monasteries across Spain from the 13th century onward. The Franciscan influence in Carabanchel dates to the medieval period, when religious orders played a central role in the administration and spiritual life of settlements around Madrid. The station opened in 2010 on Line 11, the newest metro line serving Carabanchel.

name: Pan Bendito
etymology_summary: Named after the Pan Bendito neighbourhood in Carabanchel. 'Pan Bendito' (blessed bread) is a traditional toponym predating the modern housing development, likely referring to the religious custom of distributing blessed bread in church. The area was formerly wheat fields (campos de trigo), making a bread-related name fitting. The Unidad Vecinal de Absorcion was built 1957-1963 as provisional housing for rural migrants. The Iglesia de San Benito (1963-64) became the neighbourhood's heart.

name: Abrantes
etymology_summary: Named after the Avenida de Abrantes, referencing the Duques de Abrantes, a Spanish noble title. The Palacio de Abrantes in Madrid (now Italian Cultural Institute) was acquired by the Dukes in 1842. Title originates from the Portuguese city of Abrantes.

name: Parque Lisboa
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de Lisboa (Lisbon Park) and surrounding neighbourhood in Alcorcon. The neighbourhood's streets follow a theme of Portuguese and European city names, including Avenida de Lisboa. The park and neighbourhood were developed as part of Alcorcon's urban expansion linking the city centre with Valderas.

name: Alcorcon Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Alcorcon. Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007) favours a hybrid Latin+Arabic formation: the al- prefix is a superstrate adoption over Latin *corcu/qorq from 'quercus' (oak), parallel to 'alcornoque' (cork oak), yielding 'the oak grove'. Alternative: pure Arabic 'al-kur' (hill/mound). The folk etymology connecting it to Alcorcon's famous pottery tradition is linguistically dubious per Corominas. First documented 1208.
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007); Corominas; Ayto. Alcorcon; Wikipedia

name: Parque Oeste
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque Oeste (Western Park) commercial and residential area in western Alcorcon. The area includes a major commercial park of over 125,000 m2 built in 1994-1996, and the Rey Juan Carlos University campus. The 'oeste' (western) designation reflects its position on the western edge of Alcorcon, facing toward Mostoles. The station serves the MetroSur circular line (Line 12), which connects five southern municipalities in a 40 km ring -- the longest single metro loop in Europe when it opened in 2003.

name: Universidad Rey Juan Carlos
etymology_summary: Named after the Universidad Rey Juan Carlos (King Juan Carlos University), established by regional law in August 1996 to expand public higher education in southern Madrid. King Juan Carlos I laid the first stone of the Mostoles campus on 12 February 1997, and classes began that October. The Mostoles campus houses the School of Experimental Sciences and Technology (ESCET), the School of Computer Engineering, the University Senate and the Rector's office, serving as the institutional heart of a university that has grown to five campuses across Mostoles, Alcorcon, Vicalvaro, Aranjuez and Fuenlabrada. With some 45000 students it is the second-largest public university in the Community of Madrid.

name: Mostoles Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Mostoles. Most accepted theory: from Latin 'monisterium' (monastery), evolving Monisterium > Monsteriu > Moster > Mostel > Mosteles > Mostoles, indicating pre-Islamic Christian monasteries. A 1144 document calls it 'Turrem de Monsteles' (Tower of Mosteles). Alternatives: Latin 'mustum et olea' (grape must and olive oil), or Arabic 'Mostel' per geographer Al-Idrisi.
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete Part IV: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/agosto_07/31082007_02.htm); Rodriguez Morales (celtiberia.net/es/biblioteca/?id=1935); Ayto. Mostoles; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B3stoles

name: Pradillo
etymology_summary: Named after the Plaza del Pradillo, the historic central square of Mostoles. 'Pradillo' is the diminutive of 'prado' (meadow), from Latin 'pratum'. The square has been documented since the 16th century as 'Plaza del Perezal'; by the 18th century it was known as 'Pradillo del Cano', referring to a small meadow near a water spout.
named_after: Calle del Pradillo (diminutive of prado, small meadow)

name: Hospital de Mostoles
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario de Mostoles, the public hospital it serves. Construction began as a private initiative in the early 1970s but stalled; the abandoned shell was purchased by the Ministry of Health in 1980 and completed to designs by Fernando Florez Plaza and Luis Lopez Fando. Health Minister Ernest Lluch inaugurated it on 25 June 1983 as the first county hospital in Madrid province. During his mandate Lluch championed the 1986 General Health Law that guaranteed universal public healthcare in Spain. The hospital was expanded in 1992, doubling its original height, and Mostoles has repeatedly petitioned to rename both the hospital and the metro station in Lluch's honour.
source: Comunidad de Madrid; Wikipedia; comunidad.madrid/hospital/mostoles; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estacion_de_Hospital_de_Mostoles; mostoles.es (pleno Ernest Lluch); madridactual.es

name: Loranca
etymology_summary: Named after the Loranca neighbourhood in Fuenlabrada, which takes its name from the medieval aldea (village) of Loranca. The village was one of the original settlements (along with Fregacedos) whose inhabitants founded Fuenlabrada in the 14th century. The toponym 'Loranca' may derive from Arabic 'luran' (valley/ravine) or from 'loranco' (a type of tree). The modern neighbourhood was developed in the 1990s as a garden city with 12000 homes.

name: Hospital de Fuenlabrada
etymology_summary: Named after the Hospital Universitario de Fuenlabrada, the public hospital it serves. The hospital was created in December 2002 and opened fully in 2004-2005. Fuenlabrada had been the largest Spanish city without its own hospital, with residents previously relying on Hospital Severo Ochoa in Leganes.

name: Parque Europa
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque Europa (Europe Park), a 17454 m2 urban park in central Fuenlabrada. The park and surrounding neighbourhood follow a European naming theme, with streets named after European countries and cities (e.g. Calle Francia, Calle Belgica). Not to be confused with the larger Parque Europa theme park in Torrejon de Ardoz.

name: Fuenlabrada Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Fuenlabrada. The municipality name derives from 'Fuente Labrada' (carved fountain), referring to a Moorish-era stone fountain carved in lime and mortar ('cal y canto'). The town was founded in 1375 by inhabitants of the abandoned villages of Loranca and Fregacedos, who settled near this fountain.
source: Ayto. Fuenlabrada; Wikipedia; ayto-fuenlabrada.es; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuenlabrada; memoriasfuenlabrada.blogspot.com; toponhisp.org

name: Parque de los Estados
etymology_summary: Named after the Parque de los Estados (Park of the States), a 16730 m2 park in Fuenlabrada. The neighbourhood's streets are named after Central and South American countries and cities (e.g. Calle de Venezuela, Calle de Lima), with the main Avenida de los Estados (Avenue of the States) giving the area its name. The area was formerly known as 'La Pollina'.
named_after: Parque de los Estados (park in Fuenlabrada)

name: Arroyo Culebro
etymology_summary: Named after the Arroyo Culebro (Snake Stream), a 28 km intermittent watercourse that rises in the Polvoranca lagoon in Leganes and empties into the Rio Manzanares in Getafe. 'Culebro' derives from Latin 'coluber' (snake), likely referring to the stream's serpentine, winding course through the landscape. The area has archaeological significance, with Iron Age settlements discovered along the stream.

name: Conservatorio
etymology_summary: Named after the Conservatorio Profesional de Musica de Getafe (Getafe Professional Music Conservatory), located near the station. The conservatory was inaugurated in 2000 and is part of the network of public music education centres managed by the Community of Madrid.
named_after: Real Conservatorio Superior de Musica de Madrid

name: Getafe Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Getafe. Etymology genuinely uncertain per Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete 2007). The most repeated theory derives it from Arabic 'jata' (something long) via medieval 'Xatafi', referring to the long main street along the royal road to Toledo. Philip II's 1575 Relaciones Topograficas record this tradition. Garcia Sanchez notes the Arabic origin is 'presumed based on aspect and configuration' but not verifiable. Earliest forms: Satafi/Xatafi c.1150.
source: Garcia Sanchez (CVC Rinconete Part III 2007: cvc.cervantes.es/el_rinconete/anteriores/julio_07/09072007_01.asp); Philip II Relaciones Topograficas 1575; Sanchez Gonzalez 'De Alarnes a Getafe' (Ayto. Getafe 1989); es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xatafi

name: El Casar
etymology_summary: Named after the El Casar neighbourhood in Getafe Norte. The toponym 'casar' is an archaic Spanish word meaning a small cluster of houses or hamlet, from the noun 'casa' (house) with suffix '-ar'. It was used historically to denote a settlement too small to be called a village. The modern neighbourhood was built in the mid-to-late 1990s.
named_after: El Casar neighbourhood (Getafe, from casar: group of houses)
source: Ayto. Getafe; Wikipedia; dle.rae.es; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Casar_(Getafe); toponhisp.org

name: Los Espartales
etymology_summary: Named after the Los Espartales neighbourhood in Getafe Norte. The toponym 'espartales' refers to fields where esparto grass (Stipa tenacissima) grew. Esparto was historically an important fibre plant used for making ropes, baskets and mats across arid southern Spain. The calcareous soils of southern Madrid naturally supported these grasslands.
named_after: Los Espartales (esparto grass fields, from espartizal)

name: El Bercial
etymology_summary: Named after the El Bercial neighbourhood in Getafe. The toponym 'bercial' likely derives from 'berceo', a type of coarse grass or esparto-like shrub, indicating uncultivated scrubland. Historical maps show the older form 'Hervestial'. The area has been inhabited since the 1950s-60s, with significant development from the 2000s onward.
named_after: El Bercial neighbourhood (Getafe, from bercial: watercress area)

name: El Carrascal
etymology_summary: Named after the El Carrascal neighbourhood in Leganes. 'Carrascal' means a place or hillside covered with 'carrascas' (small holm oaks, Quercus ilex), from the pre-Roman root 'carrasco'. The neighbourhood was developed from 1981 onward with planned urbanisation, unlike the earlier unplanned expansion of neighbouring Zarzaquemada.
named_after: El Carrascal (holm oak grove, from carrasca: Quercus ilex)
source: Ayto. Leganes; Wikipedia; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Carrascal; leganes.callejero.net; planosdemadrid.es

name: Casa del Reloj
etymology_summary: Named after the Casa del Reloj (Clock House), a prominent building on Avenida de Gibraltar 2 in central Leganes that houses municipal administrative services. The building features a distinctive clock tower that gives it its name. It serves as one of the main citizen service points of the Leganes city council.
named_after: Casa del Reloj (Leganes municipal building, clock tower)

name: Leganes Central
etymology_summary: Named for its location in the centre of Leganes. The municipality name most likely derives from 'legamo' or 'legano' (mud/silt), as recorded in the Relaciones Topograficas of Felipe II (1576), where town elders explained a lagoon with much silt existed at the town's founding site. Originally named 'Legamar' when founded in 1280 under Alfonso X, the name corrupted over time to Leganes.
source: Ayto. Leganes; Wikipedia; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leganes; leganesactivo.com; secretosdeleganes.wordpress.com; toponhisp.org

name: San Nicasio
etymology_summary: Named after the San Nicasio neighbourhood in Leganes, which takes its name from the Ermita de San Nicasio (hermitage), built 1772-1780 by architect Ventura Rodriguez for the Marques de Leganes. San Nicasio (Saint Nicasius of Reims, d. 407) is the patron saint of Leganes. He was a Bishop of Reims martyred by Vandal invaders. Leganes adopted him as patron to seek protection from the plague epidemics that devastated the town, at the petition of Archbishop Cisneros to Pope Alexander VI.
source: Ayto. Leganes; Wikipedia; elartedelahistoria.wordpress.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicasius_of_Rheims; es.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Nicasio_(Leganes); leganesactivo.com
